title: Decaf: On Love and Uncertainty
author: Nabila Anjum
excerpt: Decaf
imageAlt: Cover image for Decaf: On Love and Uncertainty
content: Decaf
On Love and Uncertainty

Do you know what’s going on in their heads? Did you ever? Could you? Even if you go ask your lover, “WHAT IS GOING ON?”, one, they might not tell you the truth; two, they might not even know the truth; three, even if they tell you the truth, you might either not believe it or misinterpret it and thereby be convinced by a lie despite being told the truth, etc., etc., etc. This uncertainty has been killing me! I’m sure it often kills you too. But it shouldn’t because uncertainty is inevitable, isn’t it? It’s as inevitable as death. Does death kill you as often as uncertainty does? You must have, while taking a sip of your decaf coffee, made this casual statement, “We’re all gonna die.” The casual tone covertly says, “And that’s okay.” You don’t worry about death as it is too obvious to worry about. The same goes for uncertainty too. Accept that you will never know what’s going on in his/her head.
But did a modicum of truth, like a cow tranquilizer, ever put lovers to sleep? Lovers, who choose to love, must choose to believe a truth that reconciles love and sleep.

However, it must be harder for those, who see more than others, to pretend to believe a truth so they can love. Yet, they should continue to see as closely and deeply as they do now. They shouldn’t choose not to see in order to create room for love. After all, to get rid of nightmares, would you take a pill that would not let you dream at all? Therefore, we must find a way to reconcile love and skepticism. Let’s not try to blur our view, nor should we shut out love or kick it out when it’s already in and be condemned to loneliness for the rest of our lives. We must see and yet choose to believe one of those truths that allows love in.

So, let’s take another sip of our decaf coffee. Let’s accept that we will never be able to bridge the gap between the persons we love and the persons we know, and THAT’S OKAY. Let’s accept uncertainty as we so casually accept death because the other option is PARALYZING! Wouldn’t it be paralyzing to see death as an any-time-now, like someone awaiting death underground, hearing its paces?

title: Resurgam
author: Liana Waniya
excerpt: Freedom is a word spoken so often, yet so rarely felt. Of all the forms freedom could take, perhaps flying is the most beautiful—but only for birds. We envy the endless sky they c…
imageAlt: Cover image for Resurgam
content: Freedom is a word spoken so often, yet so rarely felt. Of all the forms freedom could take, perhaps flying is the most beautiful—but only for birds. We envy the endless sky they call home, yet are they born knowing how to fly, or do they fall before they learn to soar?

A bird with black feathers and a heart far too large for its tiny body, lived in a small forest and spent its days among trees, flowers, and butterflies together with its friends. In the quiet forest, storms come here and there, creating a lot of mess in its middle-class nest. The first storm came and took away the little bird's one and only toy. It stopped mourning its toy because of the company of its friends. But soon, it was thrown into a bottomless wall. The sound of its crying echoed inside the empty wall, but no one heard. It tried to flap its dark wings as hard as it could, taking one step closer to the surface only to be pulled three steps deeper inside. It took a long time for Hope to reach the surface, only to see that they were doing great.

Hope fell into darkness more than once. It climbed out each time with trembling wings, only to discover that the world above had continued without it. So Hope flew harder, learned faster, and carried its wounds beneath its feathers where no one ever thought to look beneath.

Every night, while the forest slept, Hope spoke to the lonely moon as though the sky were the only place willing to listen. And every dawn, before the first ray of sunlight touched the leaves, it would lift its wings toward a distant mountain that no other bird believed could ever be reached.

Almost—just almost—before Hope took off toward its dream, another sudden storm came, stole something far greater and took away its dearest. Its dearest vanished with the storm without a sound, making all Hope’s efforts in vain. Agony should have been the first thing to feel, but Hope chose to laugh.
Some losses make us cry.
Others leave us smiling, because tears are no longer enough.

Hope learned that long before it understood the meaning. For no reason, it trapped itself inside its nest and looked at the sky, the clouds, and the other birds every day while singing happily. Staring at the blue sky, Hope didn't realize when its favorite color became green.

Beyond the forest lay an endless field. At its farthest edge stood a mountain dressed in evergreen. Flowers bloomed upon its slopes through every season, and butterflies drifted through the wind as though the mountain itself were breathing. From Hope's nest, it looked impossibly far away, yet impossibility had never frightened it.

Every morning before the sun rose, Hope took flight. Across the endless field it flew, chasing the same distant peak. But there was one cruel rule to the journey; every time it rested, it had to begin again from the nest. Day after day, season after season, those tiny wings carried a dream far larger than themselves.
Then another storm came.
Hope sped up to avoid the rain. Little did it know that, in a storm, rain is not the frightening part—thunder is.
The sky spun.
The mountain vanished.
Feathers scattered into the wind.
Then—
Silence.
The frozen ground reached Hope long before it was ready.

The snow did not burn Hope. It swallowed the sound of the fall, as though the world wished to forget that it had ever fallen at all. White slowly surrendered to crimson, yet the pain did not come from the wound. It came from the silence.
Hope struggled to lift its wings, only to discover there were no feathers left to carry upon the sky.
Night settled over the field. Then came the sound of slow, measured footsteps from all the directions.
"What happened, my little bird?" A deep voice echoed through the empty field. "I thought you almost reached the top of the mountain, sweetie." The voice was deep, calm, and strangely gentle.
Fear may control the body, but curiosity can defeat it in a single blow.
Hope peeked toward the voice, a lone wolf approached through the snow, walking with a limp. With every step, a dark red trail stained the white beneath its paws.
"You are wounded," Hope said for the first time, leaving every other question unasked. “Oh, you noticed,” The wolf laughed softly. Hope nodded, forgetting the fear..
"So are you, sweetie."
It sat beside Hope as though they had known each other for years.
"How did you fall, sweetie?"
"I didn't notice the thunder."
"No wonder they call you a fool." The wolf chuckled.
Hope lowered its eyes.
"A fool?"
"Yes, sweetie. They call you that because you carry what they have long forgotten."
Hope remained silent.
The wolf smiled.
"Hope. Dreams. Courage."
After a long pause, Hope asked quietly,
"Did you once have them too?"
The wolf's laughter faded into the silent night.
"Yes, sweetie."
Its eyes wandered toward the moon.
"I simply failed to notice the trap. (A pause) Do you not love your nest, sweetie?" the wolf asked.
Hope looked toward the moon hanging above the sleeping forest.

"I do," it answered softly. "The forest is calm. It is warm. It has always been my home. But promises and dreams never allowed me to stay. Distant miles kept calling my name, teaching me to fly, to run, and to keep going, even when every part of me longed to hold on."
The wolf listened without interrupting.
"So... you are like me?" Hope asked.
The wolf smiled.

"The pack I belonged to never saw my worth. They believed every wolf must hunt. I never chased prey—I chased fear away. Every claw of fear hated me like I was a plague. That was enough for them to call me useless."
Hope tilted its head.
"Why didn't you live as your nature intended? Aren’t your claws one of those fears?"
"My nature?" The wolf chuckled. "Who decided that being born a wolf meant I had to hunt? Must I become what others expect simply because they named me before they knew me, sweetie?"
After a small pause...
"We are just... us. Living for what we choose to live for."
For the first time that night, Hope smiled.
"You are different."
"We are different," the wolf corrected gently. "We are simply ourselves."
The wind passed between them without a sound.

Night slowly surrendered to dawn. The moon faded beyond the mountains, spring knocked gently upon the world, and the pain of countless struggles sank deep into their bones, just as the melting snow disappeared into the grass. At the same time, they looked at their fading scars not as strangers, but as two souls who had survived the same loneliness in different forms.
As the first light of morning reached the field, Hope whispered,
"Who are we, if we cannot simply be ourselves?"
The wolf raised its eyes to the rising sun.
“ Who will we become when all these scars fade beneath the morning light?"
As uncertainty met the rising sun, would Resurgam become the beginning of their own stories?

title: Perfect
author: Syeda Nafisa Tarannum
excerpt: Syeda Nafisa Tarannum
imageAlt: Cover image for Perfect
content: Perfect
Syeda Nafisa Tarannum
Sheren looked around her picturesque, humble abode. Despite the modest setting of the
not-so-spacious apartment, she ensured that all was prim and proper, everything placed where
they were supposed to be, resulting in a vision that could easily be a cover for the coming week’s
issue of Architectural Digest. Every single thing looked perfect, just the way her husband had
taught her. Twenty years of marriage with Urshif had conditioned Sheren to believe everything
had to be immaculate, there was no excuse for imperfection. She felt a tinge of pride imagining
how the people she expected later would walk through the apartment, and fail to hide their
admiration for all its spick-and-span nooks and crannies.
She fluffed up the already “plushy to the core of every microfibre” cushions, slid her dainty
fingers across the tabletop she had spent hours scrubbing until it reflected the light gleaming
above, admired her recently acquired mirrors, only to pause before the heavy metal frame she
had been meaning to avoid. Still crooked. Still not sitting right. It enclosed a beautiful still from
their wedding night - Urshif seated on a high chair, looking deviously handsome, with Sheren
standing behind him still resembling the teenager she had been just two years prior to that night.
Perhaps she could try one more time to budge the frame into symmetry before people arrived,
but she had been unsuccessful before and doubted she had any strength left in her to attempt it
again. She stared at the rare sign of distortion in her house- the askew frame- for a minute or two,
sighed and moved on.
As she walked across her pantry, she flinched at the sight of her freezer, which had been
struggling since the day before yesterday, had now completely failed her. It was now emanating
the kind of smell that no amount of lemons, vinegar or baking soda could get rid of. Pinching her
nose and she walked towards the freezer, and was content upon ensuring that, functional or not,
at least the freezer looked spotless on the outside. “Good”, she thought to herself, she was sure
that  certain things would eventually lead people to this freezer and she had to make sure they
would admire how neat it looked from the outside. Almost as if it had been bought just
yesterday.
Urshif believed that no paid help would ever care for the house as if it were their own. He trusted
only Sheren to be capable of keeping the house spotless. She took upon the job with fierce
intensity, going over every sweep, every brush, every scrub twice. Urshif needed her to be on top
of things, she had been after all entrusted with the responsibilities of keeping everything- perfect.
The wobbly stool in the corner of the room caught her eye. The same stool which had once
escaped her sight , allowing the dust resting on it evade her duster. Urshif had walked into the
room and noticed the unclean surface while trying to grab something from the shelf beside it. Six
legs suffered that day. Five endured the pain, but the sixth leg—one of the legs on the
four-legged stool—bore the brunt of his wrath and broke. Urshif decided to not discard it, as
keeping it around would serve as a reminder to Sheren. She would never ever be negligent again.
Sheren had only ever cooked rice when she was living with her parents. Urshif was disgruntled
when he learnt that she did not know how to prepare half the dishes he had been listing down for
his wife to concoct at his command. Her mother once detected the strain in her voice over the
phone one night after dinner, and through call after call, she had mentored Sheren until she
turned into the most skillful cook her son-in-law claimed he deserved. Not that this prevented the
occasional outbursts, which may or may not have resulted in a scar across her right shoulder after
a hot bowl of curry was thrown at her. Nor did her  precision in measuring the spices or
elaborating the cooking techniques spared her from scornful criticisms in the presence of guests.
Today, after what felt like years, she was taking a break from cooking, as for the first time since
she had started living here, she would not have to entertain the people coming over.
Throughout the initial years of their conjugal life, Sheren tried her utmost to please her husband
who seemed unimpressed by everything she embodied. Urshif made certain that she knew he had
married below him, having compromised when it came to her looks and complexion, solely
because he wanted a “simple” wife. He was downright disappointed by the fact that Sheren’s
father, who should have been on cloud nine at having successfully snagged a true gentleman for
his daughter, had not offered him certain “gifts and presents” that any other parent would have
given out of elation.
The years that followed were laced with painful miscarriages, which were, of course, perceived
as failure on Sheren’s part. Urshif the kind and generous, upon learning after her fifth
miscarriage that she can never conceive again, did not choose to leave her and remarry. Why she
was not always worshipping the ground he walked upon baffled him, for she had failed him
while he had given her a life, which warranted a level of gratitude she could only repay by
serving him eternally.
Twenty years in, Sheren had been moulded into a mute, numb entity. Just the way it should be in
Urshif’s world. However, she had shown a sign of inefficiency- she could not fix the lopsided
frame. It required some hammering, an expertise she had unfortunately failed to establish in her
two decades of training. He begrudgingly took on the task, but the problem, apparently, was
neither in the frame’s structure, nor the placement of the hook, or skills of the expert holding the
hammer. It was her father’s. The same father whose death anniversary was just the day before,
whose voice had been ringing in her ears for weeks leading up to the anniversary, whose
memories had been burning her insides all over again as the date approached. The father who
had not been a generous  father-in-law. Had the apartment he had invested his life’s savings in
been given to Urshif, all would have been well and such a disastrous inconvenience would never
have befallen him.
Not realising that words were escaping her mouth, she had uttered a begging for not bringing her
father into the matter. Thanks to sheer luck, the hammer that flew towards her narrowly brushed
past her left ear. Urshif then stomped across the room to sit in front of the television, because his
mood had been ruined and now he needed to relax and regain composure.
Sheren stood still for a long time. Urshif, displeased as usual, did not look at her or care to see
where the hammer had landed. The television continued to play. Then, with abnormal calmness,
she grabbed the hammer with her unusually steady hand and struck the back of Urshif’s head.
Thrice. Urshif’s heart that she had clogged with calories over the years by serving him endless
successions of delicious treats, finally returned the favour and gave up without much of a fight.
Chopping him up and fitting his body parts into the freezer did not take much effort, as she had
spent years organising months’ worth of meat supplies in that very storage space. It took two full
days of relentless hard work to clean up all the mess. But the smell had been growing
increasingly intense as the freezer struggled to contain her secret. It had now wafted out of the
apartment and would soon attract the rightful attention of her neighbours. People would soon be
here - people in the neighbourhood who smelled something fishy, people who had noticed
Urshif’s absence, the police, the journalists. Everyone would come and see what a perfectly
beautiful home Sheren had maintained over all these years. Everything neatly sorted, cautiously
organised, carefully maintained. Even her beloved husband’s body, cleaned and packed with
delicate dexterity. Just the way Urshif had taught her, every single thing was just- perfect.

title: প্রথা
author: Syeda Nafisa Tarannum
excerpt: প্রথা
imageAlt: Cover image for প্রথা
content: প্রথা
সৈয়দা নাফিসা তারান্নুম

বেশ কিছুদিন ধরে কিছু দেশি-বিদেশি ‘মীম’ সামাজিক যোগাযোগমাধ্যমগুলোতে ঘুরপাক খাচ্ছে। সারমর্ম হলো—মায়েরা অনির্দিষ্ট কিছু নির্দেশ দিচ্ছেন, আর করুণমুখী সন্তানেরা দিশেহারা। মা কী চাইছেন, তা বুঝতে তো পারছেই না, আবার সঠিক জিনিসটা দিতে না পারলে বকুনি খেতে হবে, সেই ভয়েও অস্থির। আমি এমন একটি মীম দেখে সঙ্গে সঙ্গে আমার বোন মেহতাজকে পাঠালাম—“আরে দেখ! এই সমস্যা তো দেখছি সার্বজনীন!”

পৃথিবীর অপর প্রান্তে বসবাসরত আমার একমাত্র বোন মেহতাজের প্রতিক্রিয়া এলো একটি দাঁত বের করা হাসির ইমোজি। সঙ্গে সঙ্গে যুক্ত হলো কান্নারত আরেকটি ইমোজি। কোনো বাক্য আদান-প্রদান না হলেও ইমোজি দুটির মর্ম আমি পরিষ্কার বুঝে গেলাম। ব্যাপারটা হাসি-ঠাট্টার ছলে তুলে ধরা হয়েছে বটে, তবে বাস্তবের সেই ভয়াবহ পরিস্থিতিগুলোতে মায়ের তীক্ষ্ণ ধমকগুলো যে তীরের মতো এসে বিঁধত, সেই ক্ষতগুলো এখনও কাঁচা রয়ে গেছে।

এই তো আট-দশ বছর আগের কথা হবে। আমি তখন অবিবাহিত, বাবার ঘরের অতি আদরের রাজকুমারী। ইউনিভার্সিটির ক্লাস না থাকলে সূর্য যতক্ষণ না সরাসরি মাথার ওপর এসে পড়ত, তার আগে বিছানা ছেড়ে ওঠার কোনো যুক্তি যেন আমার বিধানেই ছিল না। তো, কোনো এক ছুটির দিনে মধ্যাহ্নের আগমনের তাগিদে বিছানার উষ্ণতাকে ক্ষণিকের বিদায় জানালাম। সকালের নাশতা খাব, নাকি দুপুরের খাবার সেরে ফেলব—সেই হিসাব কষতে কষতে রুম থেকে বের হলাম। বেরোতেই খেয়াল হলো, বাসায় রাতে মেহমান আসার কথা। একজন-দুজন নয়, ত্রিশজন! তার মানে, আমার মা এখন আর শুধু আমার মা নন। যিনি রান্নাঘরে তারস্বরে নির্দেশ ছুড়ে চলেছেন, তিনি একই সঙ্গে ইভেন্ট ম্যানেজার, শেফ এবং আমাদের বাসার সব গৃহকর্মীর আতঙ্কের কারণ। কোন বেলার খাবার চাইতে যাওয়া সবচেয়ে নিরাপদ হবে, সেই ভাবনার উপসংহারে পৌঁছানোর আগেই শুনলাম, মা চেঁচিয়ে বলছেন, “উঠেছেন মহারানি? এইবার গোসলটা শেষ করে অন্তত নিজের ঘরটা গুছিয়ে ফেলেন!”
“আর মা… ওই নাশতা…?” আমতা-আমতা করে জিজ্ঞেস করেই ফেললাম।
“হ্যাঁ হ্যাঁ, সেইটা তো আছেই! সবে তো বাজে বারোটা! সেই সকাল আটটা থেকেই টেবিলে নাশতা সাজিয়ে রাখা আছে। খেয়ে আমাকে ধন্য কর!”

বাবা রে বাবা! যতটা ভয়াবহ আঁচ করছিলাম, মায়ের মেজাজ তার চেয়ে বহুগুণ খারাপ—তা বুঝতে বাকি রইল না। সামনে না পড়তে পারাটাই শ্রেয়, তবে সেইটা সম্ভব হবে না কিছুতেই। সাহায্য করতে পারি বা না পারি, সাহায্যের হাত বাড়িয়ে দিতে আমি যে অতিশয় আগ্রহী, সেটা মাকে দেখাতেই হবে। লাভ বিশেষ কিছু হবে না, তবে দিন শেষে বকুনির মাত্রা হয়তো কিছুটা হালকা হবে। আমার বোনের পরীক্ষা থাকায় তাকে এই যাত্রাপালায় অংশগ্রহণ করতে হলো না। যদিও সে জানত, কোনো না কোনো ফাঁকে তার দিকেও মায়ের অভিযোগের গ্রেনেড ছুটে গিয়ে পড়বে, তাই বুদ্ধি করে যতক্ষণ সম্ভব গা ঢাকা দিয়েই রইল।
হঠাৎ খেয়াল হলো, বাবা কোথায়? তাঁর আওয়াজ পাওয়া যাচ্ছে না কেন? এই ঘর, ওই ঘর উঁকি মারতেই দেখলাম, বেচারা বারান্দায় বসে সর্বশক্তি দিয়ে কিছু একটা ঘষাঘষি করতে ব্যস্ত।
“কী পরিষ্কার করছ, বাবা?”

“আরে দেখ না! এই রুপার বাটিগুলো সেই কোন সালে নেপাল থেকে এনেছিলাম। তোর মা এত শখ করল, মেহমানদের জন্য এগুলোতে একটু মিষ্টি পরিবেশন করবে। কিন্তু কেমন কালো হয়ে আছে। টুথপেস্ট দিয়ে ঘষা দিচ্ছি, বুঝলি! দেখিস, কী চিকচিক করবে!”

আমি মুচকি হেসে সরে এলাম। হয় আমার বাবা একটু বুদ্ধি খাটিয়ে এই কাজ বেছে নিয়েছেন, যাতে মায়ের চক্ষুশূল হতে না হয়, নয়তো মা-ই তাঁকে এই কাজে জড়িয়ে দিয়েছেন, কারণ সেই একই। যাই হোক, কোনোমতে নাশতা মুখে পুরে গোসলের উদ্দেশ্যে যাচ্ছি, তখন মায়ের ডাক পড়ল, “এইদিকে আয় তো একটু!”
দ্বিতীয় ডাক পড়ার আগেই এগিয়ে গিয়ে বললাম, “বলো মা, কী লাগবে?”
“স্টোররুমে যা তো! ওপরের তাক থেকে ‘ইয়ে’র কৌটাটা এনে দে, মাংসে দেব।”

এত পরিষ্কার, সোজাসাপ্টা একটি আদেশ! কী সহজেই বোঝা যাচ্ছে যে গুদামঘরে ঢুকতেই ওপরের তাকে একটি নিঃসঙ্গ কৌটা পাওয়া যাবে, যেটার মধ্যে ‘ইয়ে’ রাখা আছে। কী রাখা আছে, তা জানা নিষ্প্রয়োজন, কারণ কৌটো নিশ্চয়ই একটাই সেখানে। ঢুকেই প্রথম ঝলকে যা দেখলাম, তা হলো—কৌটা রাখা আছে আটটি!
“মা! কোন কৌটা?” আরও স্পষ্ট বিবরণের আশায় প্রশ্নটা করে বসলাম।
“কয়বার বলতে হয় তোকে! লাল ঢাকনা দেওয়া যেটায় ‘ইয়ে’ রাখা আছে।”
লাল ঢাকনা দেওয়া মোট কৌটা পেলাম চারটি। এবার? চারটিই কি নিয়ে যাব? নাকি আবার জিজ্ঞেস করব? কোনটা কম বিপজ্জনক হবে? একটু নিচু স্বরে জিজ্ঞেস করেই ফেললাম, “মা, বড়গুলোর একটা? না ছোট?”

জবাবে পেলাম ভয়ংকর নীরবতা। তারপর জোরেশোরে পা ফেলে মায়ের হেঁটে আসার শব্দ। বড় এক ঢোক গিলে করুণ মুখে দাঁড়িয়ে রইলাম। ঝড়ের গতিতে ঢুকে মা হ্যাঁচকা টানে নামিয়ে নিলেন সেই ‘ইয়ে’র কৌটা। তারপর আমার দিকে কটমট করে চেয়ে বললেন, “একটা ছোট কাজ বললাম, তাতেও যদি একটু সাহায্য পাই! ওই আমাকেই চুলা বন্ধ করে ঘুরে এসে নিতে হলো। যা, তুই সেজেগুজে ঘরে ঢুকে বসে থাক। কিছু করতে হবে না তোর!”
অতি ছোট এই বিষয় নিয়ে মায়ের এত কড়া ঝাড়ি, আর তার সঙ্গে তাঁকে সাহায্য করতে ব্যর্থ হওয়ার লজ্জা—দুইয়ে মিলে চোখ ঘোলাটে করে দিল। মনে পড়ে, গাল ফুলিয়ে ঘরে গিয়ে বসে ছিলাম, বাবা এসে ডাক না দেওয়া পর্যন্ত।
আজ এত কাল পরও এই কৌতুকাবহ মীম দেখে পুরোনো এমন কত ঘটনা মনে করে একাই কিছুক্ষণ হাসলাম। মায়েদের বোধ হয় এটা এক প্রথাগত স্বভাব, নইলে পৃথিবীর এত মায়ের সঙ্গে আমার মায়ের মিল কীভাবে বের হলো?

মোবাইলফোনটি বিশ্রামে রেখে ঢুকলাম রান্নাঘরে। খালা মাছটা সুন্দর করে ধুয়ে রেখেছে। কষিয়ে একটু পানি দিয়ে নেড়ে নিলাম। অফিসের কিছু জরুরি ইমেল আছে, সেগুলো একটু দেখে নিতে পারি এই ফাঁকে—এই ভেবে রান্নাঘর থেকে বের হতে হতে বললাম, “খালা, দু-এক মিনিট পর মাছটাতে একটু ‘ইয়ে’ দিয়ে চুলার জ্বাল নিভিয়ে দিয়ো!”
পেছন থেকে অতি বিভ্রান্ত এক মহিলার প্রশ্ন এল, “আম্মা, কী দিমু?”
“উফ! ‘ইয়ে’ যে রাখা আছে, ওই বাটিতে—ওইটা ওপর থেকে ছিটিয়ে দিয়ো!”
“আম্মা! কী কইলেন? কুনটা ছিটামু?”
“ধুর খালা, সব তোমাকে এইভাবে ভেঙে বলতে হয় কেন? লাগবে না, যাও! আমিই করছি!”
নিজেই কুচি করে রাখা ধনেপাতা মাছের ওপর ছড়িয়ে দিয়ে চুলার জ্বাল নিভিয়ে বেরিয়ে এলাম। এত সহজভাবে বলা কথাও কীভাবে বোঝে না মানুষ, অবাক লাগে!
রুমে ঢুকতেই ফোন বেজে উঠল। নিশ্চয়ই মা।
“হুম মা, বলো।”
“কিরে, রান্না করিস? নাকি ছুটির দিন, তাই বের হচ্ছিস কোথাও?”
“না মা, রান্না শেষ। অফিসের কিছু টুকটাক কাজ আছে, সারব এখন।”
“আচ্ছা, কর তাহলে। তোর বাবার ‘ইয়ে’টা একটু পাঠিয়ে দিস।”
“বাবার কী?”
“উফ! ‘ইয়ে’টা নিলি না সেই দিন? তোর কাজ হয়ে গেলে দিয়ে দিস। তোর বাবা আজ বলছিল, তার লাগবে।”
দীর্ঘশ্বাসটা চেপে গেলাম। “ঠিক আছে মা, পাঠিয়ে দেব।”
ফোন রেখে বাবাকে একটি মেসেজ পাঠালাম, “তোমার কোনো জরুরি জিনিস কি আমার কাছে আছে, যা তোমার এখনই ফেরত লাগবে?”
বাবার উত্তর, “ওজন মাপার যন্ত্রটা। কাজ ফুরালে পাঠিয়ে দিস।”
চেপে রাখা দীর্ঘশ্বাসটি সুযোগ বুঝে এবার বেরিয়ে পড়ল। যাই, ‘ইয়ে’টা একটা ব্যাগে ভরে রাখি। বিকেলে পাঠিয়ে দেব। মায়ের কাছ থেকে আর কোনো রকম তাগিদ আসার আগেই।

বয়স হয়তো বেড়েছে ভালোই, চুলেও পাক ধরল বলে, তাই বলে মায়ের ঝাড়ি হজম করার মতো শক্তি এখনও আয়ত্তে আনা সম্ভব হয়নি। কেন যে মানুষটা একটু সহজভাবে বুঝিয়ে বলতে পারে না! ঠিকঠাকভাবে বললে তো তাঁর জীবনটাও সহজ হয়, সঙ্গে আমাদেরটাও। কে যে বোঝাবে তাঁকে!
আমি বাবা কখনোই এমন হব না। এইসব আজগুবি প্রথা আমি ভাঙবই, ভাঙব!

title: Morph
author: wallflower
imageAlt: Cover image for Morph
content: I heard sounds last night coming from right outside my bedside window. Didn’t think much of it.
Probably the trees moving.
The sounds are getting louder, it’s not the trees. I don’t know it sounds like…an animal?
Something weird happened last night, I heard knocking on the window. But it stopped after some time.
Maybe I was just sleep deprived.
Anyways…talked to ma today. She’s getting better now.
2 weeks to go until winter vacation starts. Can’t wait!
The knocking wouldn’t stop I had to go and check the window. I saw a shadow. It was the size of my
upper torso. I blinked and it was gone. Did I see correctly? I need more sleep. Exams are driving me mad
possibly.
I couldn’t sleep today because of the noises. I don’t know what it is. I feel like someone’s watching me
all the time. I saw shadows all night. It’s doing something to me.
I haven’t slept for the past 3 days, I can’t think straight.
Hell is a place in my mind. I feel myself becoming it. I see dark spots spreading across my entire body. I
itch all over but I can’t bring myself to get out. Tara came by to see me but I couldn’t let her in. I can’t
control myself. I can’t think of anything but the shadow and the knocks and the spots and…
The dark spots have turned into sharp, pointy goosebumps.
I rub my fingers against my own unbecoming.  The thing, it knows my ins and outs, it feels cathartic
Sometimes…
Sometimes I can hear it, whispering into my ear. I tried to get out of my house, I tried to get help. But it’s
stopping me.
I can’t stop vomiting today. At first it was just bile, but now there’s blood all over and I can’t stop. I
might turnover my intestines next. My eyes are burning to get out of sockets. I feel something running
right under my skin. I can see it wriggling under
There’s…fur, no, feathers growing all over me. I feel warm. It speaks to me clearly now, tells me
something about a metamorphosis.
There’s no escape; only giving in. I blackout for hours, hours my body spent doing what only God knows.
I woke with scratches all over my body today. Finally mustered up the courage to look at the mirror.
It had been sometimes since I last saw my Face
I screamed as loud as I could when I finally saw my reflection. Bloodshot eyes, pupils dilated to the size
of pennies, black goosebumps all over my cheekbones, and there it was...in place of my lips…a beak like
structure. It hurts so much to even open my mouth
Help. If anybody reads this, please look for me. Tell my ma I love her.
I am so sorry.
It’s been 20 days since I first heard the sounds, 20 days since my encounter with the shadow, 20 days
since I had any contact with the outside world.
I am no longer myself. The shadow has taken over my consciousness.
I have transformed completely into an avian humanoid, something ought to be found in a lovecraftian
piece.
I sometimes see fragments of my lost soul in my eyes whenever I can chance a look in the mirror. But
then the shadow takes over once again.
I lose my mind at nights, I don’t know precisely what it is that my body is being used for. But by the
break of dawn I return to my chambers- bloody.
This scares me because, this is not my blood.
So whose is it?
There’s no hope. It told me I’ll be gone forever by fortnight.
It told me it isn’t me who needs help, it’s everybody else.
I have never felt happier knowing that I’ll die.
My head hurts from drinking too much, yet, I dragged my legs across the pavement floor. My house is
just 3 blocks down the road. ‘5 more minutes,’ I keep telling myself.
My vision is hazy and I’m stumbling. it’s not an ideal case for me. ‘Shit my parents are gonna kill me,’ I
mutter. Shouldn’t have listened to Mahi and gone out today.
I keep walking until… I suddenly feel a cold chill run down my spine. It’s 12.40 a.m. and the streets are
completely devoid of any human life. I am the only one out. Yet for some peculiar reason I feel eyes on
me. I don’t know if my drunk mind is playing games with me so I keep walking.
The wind stops playing in my face, the trees stop moving, my vision gets blurrier. There’s pin drop
silence around me.
Suddenly,
I hear the sound of large wings flapping above me, I feel a short breeze from up. ‘There’s a bat hanging
around at this hour?’ I chuckle to myself.
All of a sudden I hear screeching, loud screeches. So loud I cover my ears with both hands and lose
balance in the process.
Falling on the ground, I hear a loud thump right behind me but… from above.
I look up. It’s really dark and I can’t see clearly but I see many branches of a willow tree right above me.
Must be older than all of us.
I don’t notice at first but there’s something darker amidst the branches. I rub my eyes to see clearer but
then I hear it again-
Thump. Thump. Thump
The sound’s nearer to me…it sounds right above me.
My heart starts pounding. ‘I’m just seeing things,’ I tell myself, feeling my breathing get heavier.
There it goes again-
Thump. Thump. Thump
This time…this time the sounds coming from right behind me.
I turn around slowly, feeling a hot, heavy breath on my neck.
There it stood, this…this thing. It’s covered in jet black feathers, bloodshot eyes, white beak yellowing at
the edges and…blood stains all over. Putrid, rotten, malignant look in its uncanny eyes.
I can’t move I am stuck with primal fear. The only thing I can do is stare. And stare is all I do. I know I will
not make it tonight.
‘What do you want?’ I ask it shakily.
It doesn’t respond. It stares into me, into my soul for a second, maybe searching for fond memories in
me, things to live for, some hope and I answer with my eyes. I plead with my eyes for I can’t open my
mouth any longer.
My suffering pleases it as a smile creeps in into its ugly visage and within the flash of an eye, everything
goes black.

title: Prussian Blue
author: Paravin
excerpt: It's all Prussian Blue.
imageAlt: Cover image for Prussian Blue
content: It's all Prussian Blue.
By itself, an unremarkable shade. It's beautiful enough to be noticeable, but
not enough to make one think twice. It simply exists. It's not my favorite
color, not even close. In fact, I particularly despise this mixture of pigments.
It won't leave me be.
My room is Prussian Blue. Blue tiles, blue cupboards, blue drawers, my
days the same. The splashes of vibrant, pastel or even dull pigments seem
to lose their way and be swept away by Prussian waves. The colours speak
to me, they tell me they made the day a beautiful canvas of vivid hues with
their pinks and purples, just for me. The weather is perfect; the sun is
shining, the skies are clear and no sign of that overbearing blue. However, I
cannot see any of it. No one can. I believe everyone just chooses to ignore
the film of Prussian that overtakes every reflection our eyes are able to
comprehend. It's as if we're all in the deep and unforgiving ocean, I seem to
be the only one unable to breathe underwater. I guess they've grown
accustomed to it. Everything is Prussian Blue anyway.
The moon’s light is nearly impossible to see, lest I squint, of course. She
tells me her glow cannot be blue, because it cannot be anything. I don't
know why she lies. I can estimate its tone, I know what it is. Doesn't
everyone?
I do wonder when the last time was, when my vision was clouded not by
this blue haze, but by the childlike wonder that appears when spotting a
uniquely flawed flower. Ones with spots that look like they were
haphazardly painted on to add distinctness. They're all the same now.
Sometimes, I can recall memories basked in iridescence, but they can only
play for so long before the blue consumes them too. It's very hungry.
It isn't satisfied with casting a shadow over all that exists under the light.
Sometimes, it chooses to steal the place of the slight colour that fights to
exist in this world. It obstructs my vision to the point where I cannot make
out the reflection in the mirror, where I cannot recognize my hands in front
of me. The blue stays this way until it can no longer. But I think it's getting
stronger. These periods of temporary blindness last longer. One day it'll
come back to me and trap me in its inescapable hold. It will be too devoted
to its hunger and I will be too tired to realize its grip is a vice, not an
embrace .
I'm afraid of the Prussian Blue. I know that someday, the blue that
surrounds me will claw through my skin and seep into my veins. It'll
consume my heart and reach every crevice of my form. Maybe it already
has. I can see her. In the mirror, I seem to be blending into my room.
I am Prussian Blue. No one will be able to see me engulfed in such an
unnatural hue, as they can't even see it everywhere else. They won't see it,
not until the blue leaves nothing left to hold, not until the blue steals the
warmth from my body.
Not until I am Prussian Blue and cold.

title: The Architecture of an Unwitnessed Life
author: blue
excerpt: There are people who enter our lives so quietly that we cannot identify the precise moment
imageAlt: Cover image for The Architecture of an Unwitnessed Life
content: The Architecture of an Unwitnessed Life
There are people who enter our lives so quietly that we cannot identify the precise moment
they begin to haunt us. They do not arrive like disasters. They arrive ordinarily: through
hallways, passing conversations, fleeting glances — the accidental intersection of two
otherwise unremarkable lives.
Then, for reasons we cannot adequately defend, they become extraordinary.
Not necessarily because they possess anything extraordinary, but because we begin to place
extraordinary things upon them. Their silence becomes a language. Their smallest gestures
begin carrying disproportionate weight, and in someone’s memory, it is etched as a
philosophy of hope.
The tragedy is that the other person may never know. They continue living their life. They
forget conversations another person has replayed for years.
Two people can inhabit the same memory without ever having shared the same experience.
We tend to believe suffering requires an event like a rejection, a betrayal or a goodbye.
However, some of the most enduring forms of pain arise from what never really happened.
There is no relationship to mourn, no promise to break, no definitive ending to make the grief
comprehensible.
How does one grieve an almost?
Or was it even an almost from the other end?
So, the mind, intolerant of unfinished things, begins constructing its own explanations. It
takes fragments and builds architecture from them. A glance becomes a window. A silent
ritual with them becomes the foundation stone. Eventually, the architecture becomes more
convincing than the ground upon which it stands.
And the person who built it begins to live inside.
However, something else happens, too. You become aware that someone is watching.
Before someone else's opinion matters to us, we are relatively free. We can be awkward,
ridiculous, excessive, ordinary. We can experiment with different versions of ourselves
without wondering which one will survive in someone else's memory.
Then the self acquires an audience.
Every action develops a possible interpretation. Every mistake feels permanent. Every
embarrassing moment becomes something that might have been witnessed and remembered.
We begin to see ourselves from the outside, through a pair of eyes whose judgment we cannot
control.
One no longer wishes simply to be liked.
One wishes to be correctly understood.
One wishes for the humiliating chapters to be contextualised. To have the strange behaviour
explained. To have the worst version of oneself recognised as an aberration rather than a
revelation.
You saw me, but you did not see all of me.
So, the performance begins.
One becomes more careful about the construction of a life that might look interesting from a
distance. One hopes that they will one day be understood for their behaviour based on how
much they have changed now. There is nothing inherently false about it, but the cruelty
begins when they must eventually be witnessed by the person whose gaze we have
internalised before they can feel real.
A life becomes a portfolio submitted to an absent examiner. Yet, the examiner never asked for
it.
We begin asking questions that appear to concern another person but are, in truth, questions
about ourselves.
What will they remember?
Have I changed enough?
What would they think of my present self?
Beneath these questions lies another: is it possible to become someone new without first
being forgiven for who we used to be?
Perhaps this is why certain people become so difficult to forget. They become attached not
merely to our desire for them, but to our desire to revise ourselves.
We mistake the two longings for one.
We believe we want their attention, when what we may want is an opportunity to stand before
them without shame. We believe we want them to choose us, when what we may want is
proof that the person we once were is no longer the only person we can be.
The distinction is difficult to perceive because both desires occupy the same body. Both can
make an ordinary day feel unbearable. Both can turn a passing notification into an event of
unreasonable magnitude.
This is why another person's happiness can hurt in ways that seem disproportionate to the
event itself. A glimpse of a life continuing without us.
However, another person's happiness is not an accusation. Perhaps freedom begins when we
can encounter a reminder without turning it into a measure of our worth. When we can wear
something because we like it, listen to a song because it belongs to us, and allow these things
to exist without the tormenting thought of how they might appear through another person's
eyes. Their judgement is not a verdict on our own worth.
We may never discover what someone from our past thinks of us. We may never know
whether they remember us fondly, despise our existence, or rarely think of us at all. We may
never receive the conversation that would place everything in its proper proportions.
However, we must accept: they do not owe us an ending.
This is not a satisfying conclusion. It offers no final correction of the past. It asks something
harder of us — that our lives remain livable even when certain questions remain unanswered.
Perhaps maturity is not the moment we finally receive the explanation we wanted. Perhaps it
is the moment we realise that even if the explanation came, it could not return the years we
spent waiting for it.
I sometimes think of the self as a house.
We spend our early years building rooms without knowing what they are for. Some are bright
and open. Others are constructed hurriedly around our fears. We leave certain doors
unlocked, hoping someone will enter and understand what we have made.
When they do not, we begin decorating the rooms they never saw.
We imagine their eventual return.
We keep the lights on.
Years pass. The house changes. New rooms appear. Old walls are repainted. We discover
windows opening onto landscapes we could never have anticipated. We meet people who sit
with us without requiring us to explain every room.
And still, sometimes, we find ourselves listening for footsteps at the front door.
Not necessarily because we want the person outside, but because we have spent so long
believing that their arrival would prove the house was worth building.
One day, perhaps, we notice the absurdity of it. We have missed entire evenings of our own
life listening for someone who may not even know the address.
So we turn off the porch light.
Not in anger. Not to punish the person who never arrived.
We turn it off because there are things to do inside.
The house was never supposed to be a monument to an absent guest.
It was supposed to be a place to live.
So, perhaps that is the quietest form of freedom was not becoming someone worth
witnessing, but realising that you were never required to be witnessed at all.

title: The Dawn
author: Labiba Hasan
excerpt: The Rosewood town  is  well known for its high peace index. People call it the City of Serenity.
imageAlt: Cover image for The Dawn
content: THE DAWN
The Rosewood town  is  well known for its high peace index. People call it the City of Serenity.
No chaos, no fight, no hurdles, just people living their everyday life. All thanks to the collective
efforts of the town people and the town government.
One night near the 16th street residential area a girl was walking. Her clothes were disheveled
and torn, her body was badly bruised in multiple places, red blood soaking her clothes and a
broken arm. She was walking almost like a sleepwalker. The outside injury was visible but her
inside was screaming yet she remained silent. People tend to forget emotions when it may be too
heavy to even bear. She passed out.
The upcoming days passed in a daze. Police came , media came and the matter was dragged to
court. Today is the final hearing. The handcuffed criminal was presented before the judge. The
criminal kept head down but could feel the people watching.
Soon the hearing started. The Judge said:
- The violent and brazen behaviour of the culprit is a threat to the town’s long perceived
reputation. The court has decided to place the culprit in The Justice Cell for breaking the
town codes of peace.
The culprit finally looked  at the judge. Her face is still swollen. She asked:
- What is my fault, my lord? They are the ones who ruined me. They are the ones who
permanently damaged my right arm . I  can’t even lift a kettle.
- Your suffering is valid but Rosewood values peace over everything and your active
decision to choose a rather unsafe area is something the court cannot overlook.
Rose looked at her father in the back. His back crooked with shame. She goes silent.
- The court is adjourned for today.
The judge declared. Rose is dragged in a chain. Tons of people and the media shaming her. They
put her in a car and drive away. She stares at those camera flashes and those judging faces. She
doesn’t see faces, only masks.
They arrive at the Justice Cell. It is a barren area covered with 50ft grey walls around it. Beside it
there is a massive field. Grass trimmed, walls painted, the field stands in a contrast to the grey,
lifeless cell building. In the centre of the field there is a stage or a hanging podium.
They hand her over to  the jailor. The jailor shows  her the cell  room she is assigned. A cramped
two bed room with a basin and an unknown  smell. She sees a girl staring  at her. The jailor
introduces her to Lara, her jailmate. Jailor  asks  Lara to  show  Rose the place and tell her all the
rules and regulations.
Lara  finally moved and came closer. Then she asked Rose to follow her. They started walking.
Lara suddenly broke the silence and said:
- You were assaulted? Your family must be in trouble. They outcast people like these.
- I know but here you are equal. No one questions anything here. After today you are not
allowed to ask anything to anyone about the outside.
- Ah.. Fine.
- Breakfast starts at sharp 8. If you come late you go hungry. Then at 9 starts chores. The
warden will explain your duties. You will find your clothes at the laundry and you can't
wear anything besides the jail clothes. Do you understand?
Rose nodded. They walk through an eerie dark hallway with a bunch of cell rooms. Some
opened, some closed. Rose suddenly notices a room with an open door. A man sits alone in the
dark room with a doll in his hand. A little penguin.
- His neighbour killed his daughter. He put the man's house on fire. He was arrested for
arson. After all, who leaves a 5 year old alone at home?
Lara keeps moving. Rose stays. She did wrong. She brought shame to her family. The whole
society blames and berates her. Everyone here is the culprit. Then why something feels wrong.
She asks:
- Lara? May I know your story?
- I said. No question about life outside.
- How long is it here?
-  You stay until those wounds feel numb. Then you sign a waiver and be free.
- Waiver?
- It means you admit your mistake and the society takes you back in.
- What if…..  I don't?
- Then…..
Lara suddenly stops in her place and looks back. She says:
- Then the Dawn comes for you.
Something in her expression stopped Rose from questioning further.
The night falls. Rose sits by the wall. Her eyes hollow. She closes her eyes. When she opens
them again she finds herself in an unknown room. The roof is moldy, cracked and leaking. Floor
cold as ice. The walls are covered with big mirrors like a maze. She panics. While calling for
help, she discovers her mouth is sewn shut with thick threads. She stands, struggling  to get a
word out. Only muffled sounds. She sprints across the room. She feels like roaches are crawling
up from her throat to get out. She tries tearing the stitches with hand. But in vain. She sees her
reflection in the mirror. Her bruised face filled with tears, snorts and blood. How pathetic she
looks. She can't look at it. But the room is covered with mirrors. How can she escape her own
reflection? She knows how. Shreds of glass are scattered across the room. Her hands are a bloody
mess. Does Rose think breaking the mirror also wipes away the image?
Rose wakes up panting. She fell asleep. She doesn’t see Lara anywhere, just a note saying :
“ I was his daughter also. My mother never knew he was married before. I just wanted to take my
rights back. But I became a convicted criminal for harassment and defamation. I didn't fight.
Because you can't win against someone who accepts silence as the only form of peace.”
~ Lara
Rose read this, folded it carefully before placing it on the bed. She goes out. In the entrance
hallway she sees a large line of people. Face covered. Like  herds moving in the same direction.
Towards the empty field with the hanging stage. She also notices the Penguin doll clutched by a
man in the row. She whispers to herself:
- Their Dawn has finally come.
She hurries to the dining hall. She can't go hungry. She takes food and sits on a bench to eat. Her
shoulder tilted in a specific direction. Her exhaustion is visible in her position. But she slowly
merges to the crowd in a grey painting.

title: EID
author: Labiba Hasan
excerpt: Once the village Molla said , “ Eid is the largest festival of Muslims. It is equally blissful and
imageAlt: Cover image for EID
content: EID
Once the village Molla said , “ Eid is the largest festival of Muslims. It is equally blissful and
pleasant for everyone”. Raju was there too.  He listened. He thought to himself was eid really a
joyful experience for all?
Today is the day of Eid. Raju was sleeping under a  bridge. There was no hurry in his actions.
He starts observing. The people, their new clothes, joyous faces. Raju doesn’t have those. His
worn out pants, oversized torn shirt, rough and flaky skin, rustic hair make him seem like a
withered flower in a pool  of fresh roses .  He stands and starts walking. Underneath his calm
face his mind was bustling. The memories of the past were flashing before his eyes creating an
unnatural sense of numbness.
Raju once had a home. A small, quiet home near the Meghna. His father was a boatman. He
remembers how he used to spend hours on the boat. The waves violently shook the boat. The
figure of his father standing tall at the edge of the boat against those waves. It has  been ages
since he felt that secure and protected. He recalls his mother running behind him across the shore
with food  to feed him. Her long  dark hair waved by the wind. He also had a sister. He tries to
remember her face everyday but the vision stays blurred. He just remembers a hand clutching his
hand and running after they stole mangoes from their neighbour’s tree. A hand gently putting a
soaked cloth on his forehead when he had fever.
3 years ago Meghna took his home along with his  sister and father in river erosion. His mother,
a new widow, driven from the loss of her husband  and  daughter  decided to  leave the village
forever. Just like that Raju came to  Dhaka with his mother on a train, without a ticket. Perhaps
this  was a reason the city never accepted them. Within 6 months his  mother died from Cholera
leaving a 7 year  old Raju to fetch alone.
Today Raju has decided to walk through the city and  see how the city built on cement and rust
celebrates eid where thousands of dreams are buried under rubbles of reality.  He notices a
family of four. Just like his own family. They are dressed nicely and are busy celebrating. Raju
tries to smile like them but his reflection on the roadside glass wall  doesn't seem polished
enough .  He stops staring and continues walking.
Raju’s  family was poor. They didn’t  get  new clothes or elaborate dinners  but Eid was peaceful.
His joy was a simple boat ride or visiting a village fair on his father’s  shoulder.  Why did fate
have to  snatch something so  simple from him? In his imagination Meghna isn’t  a river, it is a
vile, unsightly demon  that took everything from him.
What time is it , maybe afternoon who knows? Raju rests near a field. It is packed with people.
Some chatting, some laughing. Raju spots a dog amid the crowd. Hunger and thirst  clear in its
eyes. No one notices it, just like  Raju.
Today Raju finally found the answer.  Eid isn’t for everyone.
The questions remain silent. Raju continues to walk.

title: Crossroads of Thorns
author: blue
excerpt: When you look into my eyes,
imageAlt: Cover image for Crossroads of Thorns
content: When you look into my eyes,
what is it that you see?
The carefree girl you once hoped to be,
or a stranger wearing the face of your dreams?
When your thunder spills through the walls,
I search myself for the fault,
as though guilt were a language
my blood had learned before my tongue.
Mother, could I have been a better child,
or was I simply born with too many edges
for the shape you wished to give me?
I was four when you pulled me by the hair
and taught the doorway the shape of my leaving,
four when my favourite doll fell from the window.
I watched it descend, a little piece of me
learning how easily I had to let go —
of the things that meant the world to me.
I was six when the wooden sticks bloomed bruises
across the small country of my skin,
and now I wonder if every friendship I bury
is another offering laid at your feet.
You did not like the company I kept,
and so I learned to leave people
before they could become important.
Look at me now, Mother.
Look at the empty spaces beside me—
you created a wreckage in the name of a perfect daughter.
You call it love, this thorned vine around my throat,
this garden in which even my breathing must grow
according to the direction of your light.
You want me first, above every name—
crowned with a future bright enough to blind us both.
But what if my heart dreams of smaller things?
A little house, sunlight gathering quietly upon the floor,
a life that does not need to conquer the world
to justify its existence.
You say you would be happy with that.
Yet your expectations keep growing teeth.
Tell me, Mother, when did your protection
begin to resemble a cage,
and when did I learn to call its bars devotion?
I have stood at this crossroads so long
that Janus has carved two faces into my heart,
one turned towards you, one towards the door.
When I walk towards myself, your tears follow me;
when I turn back, I feel my own soul
clawing at the walls of its confinement.
What am I to do with a love
that makes leaving feel like murder
and staying feel like a slow disappearance?
You, who made your dreams out of my bones,
who buried your own name beneath the weight of mine.
You, who has sacrificed her whole life
to give me mine.
Sometimes I look at you and see something divine,
a woman whose hands could coax flowers from stone,
and I wonder if I am cruel
for remembering the thorns beneath the roses.
I love you, Mother, and I hate the shape of my hurt;
I wish I could separate the two
without tearing myself open.
You once said your sisters had sons
and you had been given a snake.
I was five, but the words took root
somewhere beneath my ribs,
and even now I feel them stirring
whenever I mistake my existence for a burden.
I try to imagine the girl you were,
the expectations that coiled around your youth.
Perhaps you were hurting too,
passing down a language no one taught you to question.
But I was five, Mother,
and I did not know how to translate your wounds
without believing they were my fault.
You tell me you were happy to have me,
and I believe you.
That is the ache I cannot pull from my skin.
How can the same hands cradle and wound?
How can the same heart shelter and suffocate?
I want to understand you without becoming
another place where your sorrow comes to live.
And still, I want to sit beside you.
But I also want to sit as far away as I can.
Your cries from the other room reach for me,
and I am torn between comforting your grief
and wanting to silence the noise of our suffering.
Tell me, Mother, how do I choose myself
when your heartbreak feels etched into my skin?
I cannot keep making a home of my own undoing,
cannot keep offering pieces of my heart
to prove that I am grateful for the life you gave me.
Beneath all this wreckage,
there is still a girl who loves her mother,
and a mother she is still trying to love.
I do not know which of us
I must leave behind to become myself.
I only know that I am tired
of disappearing in the name of love.

title: The Flowers That Bloomed From Ammu's Guilt
author: Paravin
excerpt: Ammu was a ghost.
imageAlt: Cover image for The Flowers That Bloomed From Ammu's Guilt
content: Ammu was a ghost.
The most youthful face of my mother that I know, exists only in her old
study. Blue glasses perched upon her nose, red pen in hand, hunched over
reading medical textbooks larger than my head. I would tumble into her
study, crawl onto her lap and bask in her singing. She'd stroke my hair and
play back to me the songs she had already sung to me countless times
while still studying. I would drift off to lands I can imagine no longer and
when I woke up, and it would be time to leave, my Ammu would be gone
again.
Those are the only images of my mother that I can really recall from my
earliest days. Even those memories are a bit unclear after so many years
collecting dust. As becomes a mirror in an abandoned home. However, the
inspiration I felt in those moments; They're as clear and fascinating as a
snow globe seemingly unaffected by time, the fake snow swirling around as
effortlessly as it did so many years ago.
But now that I'm older, even in my hazy memories I see something my
younger self could've never noticed. My young, awestruck eyes could never
catch the guilt in her glossy ones. The guilt of being unable to be with her
baby. The guilt of only being able to give her child time in the dark embrace
of midnight.
How I wish I could go back and hold her hands, her hands worn out with
years of mastering surgical tools, and trace over each dent and
imperfection. I'd tell her that her guilt has sown the seeds of who I am now.
Never once did I feel compelled to blame her for her position. Because
something that I've carried from my childhood, is the inspiration she gives
me. Her absence in the day never felt like neglect. Knowing she was out
there bringing children into the world, while hers were so far away inspired
my love for medicine. Her strength to study till the crack of dawn even after
such tiring days made me want to do the same. The love that cut through
her fatigue, came through her hands that patted my head, keeps me going
even now. The garden of myself has bloomed from my mother's guilt. I wish
I could have shown her this garden before her guilt became a part of her. It
walks alongside her. The garden, however, is all hers. And when it's in
bloom, all of these flowers will be addressed to her.
She's revived from her apparition status nowadays. However, the guilt has
never left her irises. Her shadow seems to slump more than she does.
Whenever she forgets a small detail, or she's late to lunch, I see it. I hear it
in her rushed apologies. No matter how many times I tell her it's okay, I feel
that her guilt enveloped her long ago. It trapped her in the remorse that tells
her she is not an adequate mother. She tells me she has no regrets, but I
can see it in her eyes. The composure grows tired of sticking onto her face
and slips off sometimes. Its fall reveals her shame.
I am my mother's daughter; I inherited her round eyes, her distinct lips, her
silly facial expressions that come out when she's teasing, and the
immovable guilt that haunts her. It flowed into me through her tight hold.
The guilt of being the nothing more than ordinary daughter to an
extraordinary woman. The guilt of not being half of all that she wants me to
be. As her grievances show in her eyes, I believe mine have transfused
into my form. The garden of my person is a product of my mother's endless
guilt. But it could never be her fault. She could've never known her
resentment towards herself would become genetic. And she must not know
now. These thorny flowers are far too dangerous even for her experienced
hands. They can pierce through my skin and draw blood as I hide them
behind my back, I will sweep away the blood that drips down so it may
never reach my daughter. This guilt will end with me, and so I will never
hand these flowers over to her. She can never know the parts that will hurt
her.
And if carrying her share of prickly stems will free her from her pain, I will
tattoo red all over my hands so she must never see the blood drawn from
their thorns.
