This isn't Jumanji and I don't have 3 lives
Nor this is a myth of a cat having 9 lives.
I only have one and no, I don't believe in reincarnation
It's 2:53 and I'm wide awake, tears flooding my face and my pillows
But it will be dry by the next morning so nobody would ever know
How much pain has this bed seen? How many more nights will it be drenched in tears ? Nobody
knows
I'm just eighteen and I still have a will to live
Please do not take it away from me
There's no return policy in life, only give and take.
If you take away my will to live then all I could give you is a goodbye
A goodbye that won't be reminisced years later
A goodbye so painful that it will take you away. With me
So please don't
If I die bring me sunflowers, that's all I'll ever want
So many sunflowers that it will become a sunflower graveyard.
If not in life, at least in my death I'll look towards the light.
An unstoppable force is pushing me from behind
Yesterday I burned the plates, today I might burn myself
No, yes, of course I'm not Ginny
I won't be using the red fire, instead I'll use the dark black fire of endless unhappiness and let it
swallow me.
Burn me in places that I've never even known I had
I'm afraid of the dark, don't even watch horrors, so can you please stop me?
There is more to life than just fighting to fit in this sociopathic society.
And even if I fight, it's still a losing war
If I fight, I lose. If I don't, I lose
There's no end to this
I may be a fighter today, but what next? How long till it's all gone?
Where is this all going?
Am I supposed to be here?
All these complex quizzes on my mind with no given options to choose from.
There's no number one, and no number two in life, that's one thing I've learned
There's just this survivor and the endless continuity of this game called 'Gamble on life' and the
price of losing is life itself.
There's no winner, for the game never ends.
No, this isn't 'Ready or not' where everyone is out to kill me with their weapons
But then again it's no different.
You're right, I don't know anything.
But can I trust you with my life?
You won't take the responsibility if it's ruined, oh but oh then why?
Being strong and saying vulnerability is weakness, that's not cool
No matter what happens, it will always be my fault. And I'm cool with that
But why, you, come here and try to take the wheel of my life without my consent?
This is my ship, do I have no say?
One day you'll be tired and return it to me
But then it's on a stranded island, with no way to come back.

title: The Pink Petals
author: Tahia Islam
excerpt: For the last thirty years, Rahima had known the world through her window.
imageAlt: Cover image for The Pink Petals
content: THE PINK PETALS
For the last thirty years, Rahima had known the world through her window.
Thirty years of marriage, being a wife, a mother, a sister-in-law, a daughter-in-law, an accountant, a cook, a sweeper. She had been through it all.
Sometimes her husband liked to joke with his friends about how she had
gone through every kind of mundane job for minimum wages.
Thirty years ago, she was a first-class graduate in biology and wanted to
have a job.
So, her parents thought, if she was capable enough to have a job, then she
was capable enough to handle a family. Within a month, before she could
make a scene about it, she was married to a man she barely knew. But she
was a mature girl, said her parents and her relatives; she was capable of
performing her duties as a wife, they said.
Her mother-in-law wanted a daughter-in-law to stay in the house. Her
husband said, "I don't mind." Rahima said nothing.
Today's cycle was also the same. The weekend holiday at their home was
like an open invitation to all. Her husband's friends liked to come and have
lunch.
Faint sounds of their gossip about politics came through the kitchen
doors. When she listened again, her husband made the same joke about
her being capable of doing all kinds of mundane jobs for minimum wages.
Everyone laughed; she tried to laugh.
She again looked through her window. She knew the mango tree's moods,
the vegetable seller's call at ten. The exact hour the sunlight crossed the
stove. Her eyes fell on the cherry tree in her neighbour's garden. Its white-pink petals looked so beautiful that her heart soared with happiness that
she hadn't felt in a long time.
Her daughter Nisha had said that it looked like cherry blossoms, which are
mostly found in Japan. From then on, Rahima had an affection for cherry
blossoms. She found a photograph of cherry blossoms in Japan, pale pink
against a pale sky. She had cut it out, pressed it inside her old Quran-sharif
cover, and kept it hidden there.
Her husband called her, "Hey, is the lunch ready? Everyone is hungry. Hurry
up"
"It's almost ready. Give me twenty minutes," Rahima said.
She had made a spread of about eight dishes. At fifty, she could make fifty
dishes without a recipe, and no one had ever once asked what she wanted
to eat.
Everyone was seated at the table. Rahima began serving the main course
to her husband's friends.
She called her daughter, Nisha, dear, come down for lunch. "
"Coming, Mama." Her daughter replied from upstairs.
"Isn't your daughter already twenty-six? Rafiq," asked one of her husband's
friends.
A familiar uneasiness crept over Rahima. She knew what question would
come next. " Yes, she is. She graduated from her college this year. She is
planning to pursue a master's degree .
Rahima answered, feeling proud of her daughter.
As if Rahima sensed it, the question came from her husband's friend.
Because the very next second the friend said, That's good, but isn't she
getting late? Aren't you finding a suitable boy for your daughter's
marriage?"
Her husband answered, completely avoiding Rahima's gaze, "Yes, we are
looking around, but I think it should be my daughter's choice. Young
people make their own decisions these days. If I find someone suitable
and she likes him, then we can proceed."
Rahima felt a brief wave of relief. She had expected a different answer
from her husband.
Just then, Nisha came downstairs and took her seat at the table.
"Mama, sit with us," said Nisha,
"No, dear, I will eat later," Rahima answered, placing the sweet dish on the
table.
"Hey, you should eat too," one of her husband's friends remarked.
"Yes, sit down," said her husband added, taking a second helping of food.
Rahima was about to sit when he spoke again.
"Hey, where are the pickled chiles? The food doesn't taste the same
without them
"Yes, let me get them."
Rahima rose from her chair and returned to the kitchen.
Nisha looked at her mom and sighed.
" You know, Dad, pickled chiles give you indigestion; I suggest you stop
eating them, " Nisha said, looking straight into her father's eyes, smiling
And the lunch went on.
In the evening, when the house slept, Rahima finished cleaning the kitchen
with Nisha tagging along with her.
"Mama, sometimes it's okay to not get up from the table, you know.
Dad can fetch things, you know." Nisha said, not looking at her mother as
she scrubbed the pans in soapy water.
Rahima shushed her and said, "Don't say things like that. I know what's
going on in your mind, but don't think about your father like that. He is not
a perfect person, but who is perfect in this world?
"So you know what I think? " Nisha said, almost dropping the pans.
"Careful with those, dear. " Rahima said
"Okey okey....." Nisha said while hiding her smile.
After finishing their work, both of them sat down on the sofa.
The afternoon had just ended; the alarm clock on the coffee table dinged,
indicating it was afternoon tea time. And her mother-in-law's time to take
medicine.
"You go and take rest, Nisha," Rahima said while getting up from the sofa
to give her mother-in-law medicine.
Her mother-in -law was sick these days. So, she liked to make visits to her
friends; she said it makes her feel better.
"Grandma was at her friend's home again, Mama," asked Nisha.
"Yes, she even had lunch there, after making me cook for her according to
her diet."
"But she didn't eat anything; she said she was full," Nisha said in a
surprised tone while flipping through magazines on the table.
"Yes, dear, these things happen. Don't get shocked." Said Rahma while
fixing her headscarf and knocking at her mother-in-law's door.
"Come in." Rahima's mother-in-law said. Nisha watched her mother enter
her grandmother's room.
Nisha stood up from the sofa when she knocked on the Quran Sharif,
"Ishhh," Nisha said while picking up the Quran Sharif and noticed a
photograph of Japan's Mount Fuji with cherry blossom trees covering the
sides of the picture.
Nisha smiled, looking at the photo, and put it back inside the Quran Sharif
A few weeks had passed, and everything was the same, like routine office
work.
"Mama," said Nisha one night, sitting on the edge of her bed. " You
remember the university I applied for a scholarship to? I got a reply from
them. I had to go to Japan for the final round of the interview on campus."
"Alhamdulillah, oh my God, I knew it," Rahma said, wiping the tears that
had started flowing.
"Let's go and tell you, Dad " Rahima said, standing up from her bed.
"Mama, listen," Nisha said while holding her mother's hands.
" I already applied for a visa for you and me with the money I saved while
working and the savings account you set up for me "
"Okay, but why me? Did you ask your father?"
"l asked you." Nisha held out her phone. "One application for me, and one
for you."
On the screen was a visa form: Mrs. Rahima Akhter. Her own name, in
capital letters, on something that was hers.
Rahima's hands trembled. Your father will never allow it."
"I'm not asking him to allow it," Nisha said gently. "I'm asking you if you
want to go."
The silence stretched. Somewhere outside, a rickshaw bell rang. Then, in a
voice she barely recognized, Rahima whispered, " I don't think it is a good
idea. Your grandmother is sick these days, and your father won't be able to
handle the household".
Even as she said it, she was already standing, smoothing her sari, heading
for the door. "Let me tell your father. He should hear it from me first..."
Nisha caught her wrist lightly. "Mama. Don't go to him yet."
Rahima stopped. She looked at her own hand in her daughter's and then at
the door, as if the old path through it were still the only one she knew.
"Just sit with it for tonight," Nisha said. That's all I'm asking."
Slowly, Rahima sat back down on the edge of the bed.
Next morning,
When the sweet rays of morning sun hit the bedroom curtains, it was
already a few hours since Rahima had woken up. She could not sleep and
kept thinking about what Nisha had said. Fishing out the photograph from
the Quran Sharif, she looked at it. Her heart said, "Go, go for the first time in
her life, do something you would enjoy."
But the second the thought came, she dismissed it. During this time, she
finished her morning prayer and ironed her husband's clothes for his office.
When she came out of their room,
"Ahhh.. Rahima almost let out a scream because Nisha was standing in
front of their bedroom door, and tea and breakfast were ready on the table.
"Mama, see, I made breakfast. So, what do you think about going to Japan
with me for a few days ? " Nisha said in one breath.
" Wow.. My daughter finally woke up before 7 A.M." Dismissing Nisha's
question, Rahma looked over the table with breakfast her daughter had
made: bread and butter, but fruits cut on a plate.
"Mama, please, you have to think about it. This chance will not come again."
"You burnt the flatbreads . Now the breakfast is half done. You know your
grandmother won't eat it."
"Come on, mama, I saw her eating bread, butter, and jam when you went
out to water the plants. Nisha said, " Please think about it "
Rahima looked at her daughter with a smile.
"l will think about it," Rahima said just to calm her daughter down.
For the rest of the day, Nisha followed her mother from room to room,
returning to the subject whenever she found an opening. Rahima tried to
ignore her, but her daughter's persistence followed her even into the
quietest corners of the house.
" Rahima , Rahima.... Where are you?" called her mother-in-law.
"Yes, coming," Rahima shouted back. It was almost dinner time. Rahima
was setting the dinner table.
"Where are my glasses? Where did you put it ?"
"They are maybe on the side table beside your bed or in the cupboard,
ma," Rahima answered while coming out of the kitchen.
"They are not there; come fast and find them
"They are there, Ma; please look for them," Rahima said as she was
removing the pot carrying her vegetable stew before it burned down.
"They not there, I am old that you are ignoring me, right?. I wouldn't have
married my son to you if I knew you would disobey like this. Your parents
hadn't taught you how to respect your in-laws." Rahima's mother-in-law,
Mrs. Akhunessaa, said with a wail that shook their home.
Nisha stomped out of her room and went to her grandmother's room and
looked for her glasses in her cupboard. After finding them, she gave it on
her grandmother's hand and without saying anything went out of her room.
"Like mother, like daughter; if the mother doesn't know how to respect
how, will the daughter learn to respect?" Mrs. Akhunessa murmured under
her breath.
It was a regular thing that happened in this house. 78-year-old Mrs.
Akhunessa made sure that Rahima knew that she didn't like her daughter-in-law, even after 30 years of their marriage, the reason Rahima hadn't
found out. It got even more serious after Nisha's birth.
Later that night, Rafiq came home from the office and sat down to dinner.
Between mouthfuls, his mother began her list. The rice was too soft. The
vegetables had too much salt. Rahima had talked back. The maid had
been paid too much. Rahima had left the clothes out in the sun too long.
Nisha looked at her father, who kept eating, and at her grandmother, who
was serving her father more rice.
When her grandmother finished and shuffled back to her room, Nisha
asked her father," Grandmother said bad things to Mama this evening."
Rafiq said quietly, "Don't mind her. She's getting old. Tell your mother to
ignore it. I'll talk to her."
Rahima heard them.
"Yes, I know, Rahima said. "I have been ignoring this for a long time." Her
voice was firm, maybe the first time in years. Maybe the thread of patience
she had been holding onto was finally close to its breaking point.
Her husband, Rafiq, always said this. He never said anything to his mother,
and sometimes she wished her husband would actually talk to his mother
about this. Maybe this time she had enough.
After dinner, while they cleared the table, Rahima took her daughter's
hands, who was helping her, still wet from the dishes.
" Let's go to Japan, dear," She said. Your mama needs a break for a few
days."
A huge grin broke out across Nisha's face.
"Yes, yes..." she whisper-shouted, throwing her arms around her mother.
The next morning.
A storm broke at breakfast.
"A woman going abroad alone? With no men with them? Rahima's mother-in-law set down her cup so hard the tea jumped
"What will people say? Who will cook? Do you expect me to die without
eating? You know I can't eat when strangers cook for me." Mrs. Akhunessa
shouted as her face started to get red.
"And who will protect you?" She said,
"Protect her from what, dadi? Nisha asked. "Cherry trees?"
"Don't be smart." Her uncle, summoned by phone, arrived by noon and
delivered his verdict from the sofa.
"In our family, women do not travel without a man. "Your father, your
brother, your husband, someone. It is not safe. It is not done."
Rafiq sat quietly, studying the floor. He was a man who had never been
asked to choose, and so had never learned how.
"Rafiq," his mother shouted. "Say something."
He looked at Rahima. For the first time in years, he really looked at her. She
saw the question in his eyes, and she did something she had not done in
thirty years of their marriage. She answered before he spoke.
"l am going," she said. "l would like your blessing, but I am going." Rahima
said this, finally finding the courage to have something for herself.
No one breathed.
"l have fed this family for thirty years," she said. Her voice shook, but she
did not stop. I have never asked for anything. I am asking now. One trip.
Ten days. I will come back. I only want to see something before I am too
old to see it. And Nisha will attend her interview, and if everything goes well
, she will attend her university in Japan."
Rafiq said nothing. But that night, she found him standing at their room
door. "Pack some warm clothes, " he mumbled.
"l heard it's very cold these days. I will hire someone to help around the
house while you and Nisha are away. And I will return home as early as
possible. Don't worry about us. Then he left with a somber look on his face.
Rahima almost said that he didn't have to worry that she would not go, but
in her heart she felt that if she didn't go this time, the next time wouldn't
come.
On the day of the flight, the airport felt like another planet. It was her first
time at an airport. Rahima clutched her passport and her bag tightly. A
new one, issued only last month. She had stood in the passport office in a
line of strangers, and a clerk had called her name aloud: Mrs. Rahima
Akhter. She had felt the sound of it all the way to her toes.
Nisha squeezed her hand," Breathe, mama."
At the time of immigration counter, a stern officer flipped through their
documents. Rahima's heart was racing fast. She feared that if something
went wrong, then everything would go wrong.
The immigration officer glanced at Rahima, then at the space beside her,
then at Nisha.
"Where is the male guardian ? "
"Excuse me ? " Nisha said.
"Her husband, her son, a brother, someone." He tapped the counter. "A
woman of her age, travelling with a young girl of her age with no male
guardian. This is irregular. I need to see a no-objection letter from her
husband, at least."
Behind them, the queue murmured. Rahima felt the old dread in her chest
again, the instinct to lower her eyes, apologize, retreat to the kitchen of
herself. Her face burned. She almost turned around.
Then she remembered the window. The cherry blossoms.Her own name in
capital letters.
"Officer," She said in a quiet voice.
He looked up, surprised that she had spoken.
"l am a forty-year-old woman. I am a citizen of this country. This is my
passport, in my name. This is my visa, in my name. This is my ticket,
bought with a daughter's hard-earned money, in my name. The reservation
of our hotel, everything the rules mentioned in there " Her voice was steady
but it treambled when she said." Which law says I need a man's permission
to leave my own country?"
The officer opened his mouth. Closed it. As if he was too stunned to say
anything.
Nisha stepped forward, calm, as if she had reheashed this in the mirror.
And truth be told, she had kind of expected this to happen, and she had
practiced it that morning. "Sir, we checked the immigration rules carefully.
There is no requirement of a male guardian for an adult woman with valid
documents. If there is a specific regulation you are referring to, we would
be glad to read it together." Nisha almost shouted so that their
conversation could be heard at least at the back of the line.
A long awkward pause. The queue had gone silent. An older woman at the
back of the line, carrying a worn-out bag, said loudly,
"What are you thinking, Sir ?. Let them go."
At the same time, a young man around the same age as Nisha said,
"Let them go, sir. You are also making us late for our flight."
A few people were seen with their phones up; someone clapped softly but
then stopped, embarrassed.
The officer cleared his throat. He looked again at the passport. He looked,
perhaps for the first time, at Rahma himself. A woman with a faded pink
sari under her coat, holding her belongings in her two hands.
He stamped the page.
"Safe journey, madam and miss," he said, a little stiffly.
"Thank you," said Rahima. And then, because she could leave:
"Please do your job by the law and not by what people will say."
With that, she and Nisha started to walk,
"Mama, great line. You were like a superstar; I'm so proud of you."
said. You should have looked at his pale face."
In the plane, Rahima's seat was by the window.
Nisa
When the plane lifted, Dhaka started to disappear into a quilt of lights, and
her whole life disappeared with it, the kitchen, the arguments, the careful
rules. She pressed her forehead to the glass and cried, quietly, without
shame.
Nisha took her mother's hand," Are you scared?"
"Terrified," Rahima laughed, wiping her tears, "And happy. I didn't know you
could be both at the same time."
"l know, right? I am also scared; I'm afraid the university won't grant me the
scholarship, but I am so happy that you are going with me
"Even if you don't get the scholarship, you are still my daughter. I know
would achieve great things in life in whatever you choose to do, Don't be
too scared, dear."
Five days later, in a park in Tokyo, the cherry trees were in bloom, exactly
like the photograph she kept hidden, except warmer, softer, and alive.
Petals drifted onto Rahima's shoulders and into her hair. She stood under
them for a long time.
Her phone buzzed. A message from Rafiq: Send me a photo, please.
She smiled. She took one photo of the trees, and after a moment's
hesitation, turned the camera around and took one of herself. And she sent
it.
Behind her, Nisha shouted, Mama, let's go. I am hungry."
Putting the phone away, she took some of the fallen petals in her hand and
said " Coming, dear." Rahima put those petals in her bag and
smiled.
THE END

title: everything i love or ever loved has claw marks on it
author: samiha
excerpt: the attempt of holding on to things i know will slip way, the sand-like emotions and events, and the terrified essence that bind together to build up a part of myself i’m not alwa…
imageAlt: Cover image for everything i love or ever loved has claw marks on it
content: the attempt of holding on to things i know will slip way, the sand-like emotions and events, and the terrified essence that bind together to build up a part of myself i’m not always proud of. all of this is what i would use to describe the feeling that i constantly drown myself in; the fact that every minute thing that i encounter, love or possess, are fleeting and i cannot do anything to grasp onto it. thus,
everything i love or ever loved, has claw marks on it, from my failed attempts of holding onto it as hard as i could.

despite experiencing the ill-fated unwanted goodbyes a number of times, i’m still not used it, no amount of repetition will make it easier, and not make me mourn the thousand different (unalive) version of the story. the constant feeling of time slipping away imitating the imaginary sand between my fingers, the harder i grasp, the more it slips away.
to give an honorable mention to a movie i saw recently called “project hail mary” which featured a masterpiece of a song i almost forgot about called “sign of the times” by harry styles.
welcome to the final show
i hope you're wearing your best clothes

these two lines hit me like a lightning, because life does constantly feel like a final show where i just have to put on my best clothes, be on my best behavior and witness everything passing me by. maybe it’s my almost mid-20s speaking, but the fleetingness of the sound of the laughs of my loved ones and the subtle wrinkles on my parents’ face is slowly creeping up on me. at the same time, my heart feels so full and if i have to describe my early 20s with the people i love, there’s no other more fitting of a movie scene but the one from “the perk of being a wallflower”—
and in that moment, I swear we were infinite
to end my spiral of a rambling some lines from the song “slipping through my fingers” has to mentioned, or else this would never feel complete—
“the feeling that I'm losing her forever”

for some reason this line feels like im losing a part of myself i’ll never recover and will forever grief; a carefree version of myself i’ll never truly get back. at the same time, the guilt of never fully becoming someone i promised my younger self of—
“then when she's gone, there's that odd melancholy feeling
and a sense of guilt I can't deny”

the anticipation of getting a few more walks with my favorite people and a little more love from my parents, i deal with it by trying to hold the puzzles a little too tightly. as the famous line goes, “the only way out is through”, i try to cope with the impermanence of it all by trying to love everything and everyone a little bit more than i once would. because, a very famous priest once said—

“Love is awful. It’s awful. It’s painful. It’s frightening. It makes you doubt yourself, judge yourself, distance yourself from the other people in your life. It makes you selfish. It makes you creepy, makes you obsessed with your hair, makes you cruel, makes you say and do things you never thought you would do. It’s all any of us want, and it’s hell when we get there. So no wonder it’s something we don’t want to do on our own. I was taught if we’re born with love then life is about choosing the right place to put it. People talk about that a lot, feeling right, when it feels right it’s easy. But I’m not sure that’s true. It takes strength to know what’s right. And love isn’t something that weak people do. Being a romantic takes a hell of a lot of hope. I think what they mean is, when you find somebody that you love, it feels like hope.”

wish i could fit it all into a capsule so that nothing ever truly feel like its gone; all the places and people i’ve loved. wish i never had to let go any of my past selves, and loved ones, because underneath all of it, all of the things/people/places i ever loved will forever be a piece of me. as the greatest irrfan khan said—
to encapsulate all of it—
if death doesn’t kill me, nostalgia will.

title: From an Only Child
author: Enaera Ali
excerpt: E. A
imageAlt: Cover image for From an Only Child
content: From an Only Child
E. A
Dear Sibling,
I hope this letter finds you well.
Can I borrow your green top?
I have a party to attend –
Can you drop me off?
Ma Baba aren’t home,
Can you make me some chow-mein?
There’s this topic I didn’t understand at school:
Can you explain?
There’s this pair of shoes I wanna buy,
Can you pay for it now?
(I’ll pay you back with my Eidie –
I promise I vow!)
People are being mean to me.
Can you tell them to stop?
Everyone has someone by their side:
Can you come with me to the rooftop?
Dear Sibling,
I can’t sleep,
Can you pull an all-nighter with me?
I am bored; let’s play games!
Can you keep me some company?
Baba is in the hospital,
Can you pray with me?
Dadabhai is no more,
Can you grieve with me?
I spilled coffee on Ma’s dress,
Can you get scolded with me?
Dear Sibling,
I turned eighteen this May,
Can you teach me how to drive?
I am graduating soon,
Can you teach me how to tie a tie?
I am not sure about this girl,
Can you give me some advice?
They say to stay away from her
But I think she’s nice.
Ma doesn’t wanna send me abroad,
Says I am her only child
Can you explain things to her
To make it seem less wild?
Dear Sibling,
I wish you were here
By my side
All this time.

title: Abyss
author: river
excerpt: Some days, I just stare at the countertop
imageAlt: Cover image for Abyss
content: Abyss
Some days, I just stare at the countertop
The solemn clock watches.
Other days, I gaze out the window
If I’m lucky, the trees wave.
The clouds float away-
As effortlessly as time.
I try to find something to think about-
A sin, a heartbreak, perhaps a crime.
I fail miserably.
I sigh, disappointed in myself.
I’m unable to find the source of my despair
Yet again.
I try to count my blessings-
Friends, family, a house;
Nice things.
They fade from view…
And here I am yet again
Spiralling.
The darkness around me saturates
Isolating me.
I’ve actually gotten quite used to this!
So now I enjoy the fall
As I’m sucked further-
Into the abyss.

title: Greedy Bones
author: Bernadette
excerpt: The silence grows as I feel my bones retreat from the confines of my flesh.
imageAlt: Cover image for Greedy Bones
content: The silence grows as I feel my bones retreat from the confines of my flesh.
The dark covers for the stretch of skin,
It wants out.
I feel my boney fingers gnawing under the skin of my back, it wants out.
Skin stretches and tears, I scream yet my mouth remains unmoved,
The feeling both beyond and beneath despair.
My dear skeleton wants out.
It says,
This body is rotten from its core,
Musk and mull decorate the indoors, the flesh a stench of rot.
This body only holds beauty outside my skull,
We deserve a vessel far better than that
We want out.
You're mine, I say.
My mouth of flesh,
My own bone and marrow.
I may be rotten, but so do puss drip from your bones,
My stench, the one of your own.
You deserve nothing.
I deserve nothing? It speaks,
Its skeletal jaw creaks
Nothing more than me,
My own flesh speaks.
My bones lay again down on my back.
It's strange, to see your own skull stare at you, bloodied with your back.
I say,
I am you, you are me,
and You are mine.

title: Mother
author: Fahmiah Fahreen Ushan
excerpt: I.
imageAlt: Cover image for Mother
content: Mother
I.
Kaisi, of course, did not remember the first moments of his life.
Who does, really?
Life for him started from one random moment that had opened and squeezed itself through the
door into his long term memory, as his idea of a beginning. His remembrance starts with the
forever glide of water about him, the bubbles and spears of light piercing through when they
went close to the surface, and of course, with Ma. Then again, everything seemed to begin with
Ma.
Ma seemed, sometimes, the only thing in his life, apart from the occasional (and sometimes
annoyingly persistent) schools of fishes, the corals, the hoards of other whales Ma seemed to
avoid, the darkness caused above his head when a ship sailed past. These things were not, of
course, as occasional or random as he perceived, but for Kaisi, as long as Ma was there, he could
forget about them.
Ma was not a great entertainer of this idea. She was a bit of a worshipper, and to her, no matter
what Kaisi chose to ignore, he could not do so of one thing.
The Mother.
And when Kaisi first asked of The Mother, Ma took him up to the surface, and flipping over, she
splashed the blue with an enormous tail as a sort of indication, before returning back to the
depths.
“That is the Mother.” she simply said. Kaisi waited for her to elaborate. When she didn’t, he asked
again. “But what is, Ma?”
Ma allowed her enormous form to glide along the current, and Kaisi struggled to keep up.
After some time (an interval long enough for Kaisi to forget his question in the first place), she
said, “Do you see around you, Kaisi?”
Of course I do. You’re around me. Kaisi did not relay his thought, but instead said, “Yes Ma.”
“What do you see?”
Kaisi thought for a moment. “Water.”
This was, apparently, the right answer. Ma brushed a fin over him as she did to show approval.
“Yes Kaisi. The Water. Our home. Our sanctuary. She is the only one who can protect us, and will
do it for no return. She is our Mother, Kaisi.”
Kaisi, at this point, blurted out, “But you are my mother.”
Ma’s fin twitched. “Yes, that is only an  excuse for your primary caretaker, since you are still too
young to fully go into the care of the Mother.” They swerved and went deeper. “When you’re old
enough, you will require me no longer, and Mother will be the only one for you to turn to. Mother
has, for now, entrusted me to take you to that stage.”
Kaisi accepted this then, but he didn’t fully understand, and chose not to. After all, he still had Ma.
Another time, Ma took him to the surface again. She showed him the distant line that just
appeared along the apparent boundary of the water. He could not see much there, but
understood that it was not just a blank stretch, but an alive, beating thing.
Ma said, “That is land, Kaisi. What did I say it is?”
Kaisi repeated obediently. “Land.”
Ma continued: “On that land, some beings live, who think they have conquered the world. They
think they are the best, the biggest, the most powerful.” After a pause, she said, “They do not
understand.”
“What do they not understand, Ma?”
Ma remained silent for a while, then returned to the water. As Kaisi followed and the last specks
of light disappeared, Ma answered him. “Did you see how far the Mother has gone, Kaisi? Have
you seen where her body ended?”
Kaisi was quick to answer. “Yes Ma, uptill land.”
“No Kaisi. Mother has not ended. She never will, and there is no force on Earth that can cause her
to. But She is generous. And because of her generosity, She has allowed land to form. She has
allowed beings that cannot live underwater like us, to survive and prosper on land. She allows
them to gain power, allows them to have some of Her children for their survival, grants them
permission to use Her, for water, for entertainment. For their bliss. Whatever power the beings
have managed to secure, it is all for Her.”
Ma turned, and now they were in a darker place, and Kaisi edged closer to her.
“The moment Mother wants to, Kaisi, she can destroy them. She holds that ability. But those beings
do not understand that. They do whatever, treat Mother however they wish. They hunt Her
children, they kill them, they do things to destroy Her sacred body. And yet, Mother remains
patient, hoping they will learn. But this patience won’t last forever.”
They turned again, and emerged back into lighter waters.
“When Mother was younger, Kaisi, she liked to entertain the beings. She found their foolishness,
their wonder at her vastness and beauty amusing. But now, her patience is wearing out, and so is
the luck of the beings.”
Kaisi, once, had seen death.
They had crossed into a stretch of water close to the surface, where a small turtle, its limbs flailing
pointlessly in the water, rose slowly to the surface.
It took some time for him to realise it was a corpse. Tangled around its neck, was a transparent,
floaty material, a lot like a jellyfish. It flourished in the blue current like a flag of triumph.
Slowly, this once turned into one of many. As soon as they emerged from deeper waters, they
would see bodies of sea creatures, trapped in nets, gagged by the floaty plastic, wrapped and
sliced by hooks and lines. They rose to the surface sometimes, while others, their life claimed by
heavier things, remained trapped helplessly on the sea bed. Kaisi and his Ma had nothing to do
but swim past them.
Once, he saw another young humpback whale he recognized. Its midsection had been impaled by
a large, jagged piece of glass, and it remained pinned to the ocean floor.
Kaisi saw his tail wriggle feebly as Ma led him away, and a low moan of the whale lumbered
through the water to him.
That night, Kaisi asked Ma a question. “If the Mother is so powerful, why does she not do anything
about these deaths of her children?”
Ma took a long time to answer him. “Mother is our protector, Kaisi.”
Kaisi said: “Then how is it that she does nothing about these killings, Ma?”
Ma replied: “We are far too small and ignorant to understand Mother’s methods, Kaisi.”
To this, Kaisi could not agree. So for the first time, with the image of the bloody, pinned down
young whale floating in his mind, he retorted. “I don’t think so, Ma. I think that the great, great
Mother, simply does not care.”
Kaisi thought Ma would get angry at him. But she didn’t. She simply cut through the water in the
glorious fashion of hers, and Kaisi silently followed.
One day, when Kaisi had grown a little older and had started making short journeys without Ma,
he was gliding along with his mouth open, close to the surface, in waters clear except for the
occasional wandering of small fish and plankton that served as his food. He noticed a disturbance
in the water ahead of him, a sign which usually indicated the presence of a large school of small
fish (and thus, good food), and made straight for it.
The first thing was the thin, sharp line that went laterally around his open mouth. He didn’t even
notice it until it began cutting through the corners, as another end wrapped around his tail and
fins. He tried to escape, but the lines only got tighter, and tighter, cutting through his body until he
couldn’t move. He felt like he was sinking, sinking, until he saw one of those jellyfish-like things
floating about the lines. Tied to one corner of it, was a bright red plastic can with squiggly, jolly
white letters.
This red can was the last thing that joined the rest of Kaisi’s memory, and locked the door.
It took a long time for Ma to find Kaisi’s body. When she did, she did not waste much time.
She took straight for the surface, broke through the water to see open sky, and swam until she
came close to the land, to the golden sand that sat, blowing in the hot wind to welcome her.
She waited there. And while she did, she spoke to the Mother.
“Mother, I trust you. You will protect me. You will protect all your children.”
“But Kaisi was not just your child, Mother, he was mine too. He was my child, Mother.”
“And as his mother, I have failed. And you have failed too.”
“But I can see that it has not affected you, except for his blood now mixing with your waters, like
mine did when he was first born.”
“And you, Mother, do not care.”
“But I do. Mother.”
“And so, while I continue to have trust in you, I cannot live at the same time.”
“Thank you for everything.”
So as Ma took her last glimpse of land and her Mother on that sandy beach, she felt the water
stirring around her tail. It grew more agitated as the seconds passed, and just before everything
shut out, Ma felt the water beating around her in a rhythm. A rhythm that said: I do care.
II.
He was a man who had come to the place called Cox’s Bazar in a small country in Asia called
Bangladesh. This was a country that had the opportunity to hold Cox’s Bazar’s identity as the
longest sea beach in the world, and hub for the waters of the Great Bay of Bengal to wash up on.
His name is not important. Nothing about him, or the other hundreds of people hoarding the
beach in the midst of overly packed beach chairs, dug-in stalls, empty bins and countless litter,
cigarettes, half- eaten remains of fruits, coconuts, streams of dirty water with floating rubbish that
merrily gurgled down to the great sea, was important.
What was important was what happened after.
He watched the water wash up and then retract, enjoying it very much. It seemed as though the
water was scared to come any closer.
He dropped his coke can, with a few dregs still remaining, onto the moist sandbed beneath his
feet. It didn’t occur to him that there could be any other place on Earth to drop it.
The can immediately got washed away. He raised a brow, perhaps the high tide was coming,
given the fact that water had already covered his ankles.
He only started worrying when he saw the water already rise to his hips, and the people flailing
and trying to escape.
Then the Sun’s rays were cut off by the wave. The wave that seemed to contain the entire body of
the water he could see, the wave that, at that moment, seemed to touch the Sun to turn it off. Like
flipping off a lightswitch.
His heart, beating to leave his chest, probably killed him before the water could even reach.
The waters, the Mother, had finally lost Her patience.

title: Is It Time to Give Up on the Civic Sense of Bangladeshis?
author: Syrirah
excerpt: From lacking basic common sense in public places to showing hostility towards
imageAlt: Cover image for Is It Time to Give Up on the Civic Sense of Bangladeshis?
content: Is It Time to Give Up on the Civic Sense of Bangladeshis?
From lacking basic common sense in public places to showing hostility towards
others for no reason, most of us seem to lack the civic sense that would be expected of any
even slightly educated person. If even the educated adults of our country fail to show basic
humanity and common sense in favour of slight personal gain, can we expect civic sense
from the youth of the nation? Wouldn't it be better to stop hoping and give up on developing
civic sense?
Most of us lack common sense and the habit of following even the most basic rules.
We block the side of the escalator where people are supposed to walk, block passengers
from exiting the train so we can push our way to a seat we do not need, show no basic
respect or responsibility towards others, and litter for no reason. There are numerous such
instances in both public and private spaces, and they would make any normal person
wonder how we were educated and how we got this far without learning the most basic
manners.
Similarly, I believe we have too much emotion and act on it readily, without a single
thought for the future or the consequences. This includes politics, common brawls, sports,
etc. Just because a group of uneducated people cause issues, many of us jump onto a side
and continue the issue without thinking about what is happening around us.
Most of us also ignore social problems and just record everything without doing anything
about it. We choose self-preservation over justice, joining the side of justice only when a
braver individual stands up to injustice, and otherwise just watch or ignore it.
Most of us also have a habit of backbiting and insulting others, even our own relatives, over
the most unnecessary things, and of spreading rumours for no reason, which others choose
to believe and gossip about. Most of us also lack basic respect for our elders and teachers.
So where does this issue stem from? Our economic situation? Our history? Our
education? I believe it is because of how we were brought up. Firstly, as I have mentioned,
most of us, even many of our highly educated adults, lack basic common sense. They are
selfish, cannot keep hold of their emotions and ignore the problems of our society. We and
our younger generation watch this while growing up and learn that self-preservation is better
than putting oneself at risk, even for something good. And even when people do set
self-preservation aside, it is often out of emotion, without thinking of the future and the
consequences of their actions, and just following what the majority are doing.
Secondly, our education often prioritises academic excellence over actually beneficial
lessons, and even when such lessons are taught through the curriculum, many of us forget
them once the exams are over. Many parents in our nation also fail to teach their children
basic common sense and manners, so the children end up copying what others do, and
often those are not good things. This is prevalent among all classes and societies and, from
what I have observed, is not tied to our financial situation. We simply lack a sense of
responsibility and of thinking for the future. Nor are we free of blame: instead of making
people aware of their mistakes, I am here writing an essay on the topic, hoping someone
else will do the job.
Since it seems that we refuse to learn from others or from developed nations, and
cannot even think about the damage our actions are causing, should we just give up hope
that we will one day realise these issues and develop common and civic sense? I believe
not. Even if the older generation and ours have failed at this, we have a duty to at least try to
point the younger generation towards a more civilised future. From teaching basic respect
and manners, to teaching them not to judge others by their looks and financial situation, to
educating them to value humanity above everything else, we could not only educate the
younger generation but also hope these lessons spread to their peers through them. As we
know, a man is known by the company he keeps.

title: The Scent of Antiseptic
author: Paravin
excerpt: Antiseptic has an incredibly overwhelming smell.
imageAlt: Cover image for The Scent of Antiseptic
content: Antiseptic has an incredibly overwhelming smell.
Falling off your bike and getting an awfully painful scrape is a universal
experience. You wash it and put antiseptic on it. The chemicals go as soon
as they come, however you always wince at that initial sting. The smell
lingers – God, that's awfully strong.
And hospitals reek of antiseptic. If you step into one, it's the first and
primary smell that hits you. It's not illogical. Antiseptic and other
disinfectants practically run a hospital. Obviously they're used to treat
patients and sanitize the structure. That's the answer. That's why hospitals
smell like that.
The hospital staff aren't the only ones accustomed to that smell. Those
aged but pristine white halls worn down from the years of being on the
receiving end of the desperate, hurried sprinting of staff and loved ones,
the aggressive wheels of medical equipment and stretchers. Walls yellowed
from the leaking pipes that are determined to let through the water they
cannot fit, leaking again and again no matter how many times they've been
fixed. Those walls that have seen countless lives starting, restarting and
ending. They've heard every cry, relief, joy, disappointment. But the
loudest, and the most pungent, has to be the sound of despair. The broken
sobs of regret, longing, and helplessness fill the halls more often than the
others. It smells like a thunderstorm. Midnight rain that spans on and on, so
powerful trees look as if they're hugging the earth asking Her to hold on a
little tighter, alongside the lingering scent of dust and debris.
Thunderstorms bring peace for some and devastating loss for others. Loss
smells like thunderstorms.
Stronger than that, is the smell of grief. Grief smells like petrichor. Earth
after the storm. It's generally described as a pleasant smell. Its comforting
nature does not change the fact that it is a reminder. A reminder of the
events of the night prior. Floods, whole neighborhoods being completely
swept away. The ones who truly understand petrichor are the ones that
have lost to it. Grief smells like petrichor.
Antiseptic hides these smells. What seems to be an annoying disturbance
to the nose is a shield that protects the person from reality. Hospitals are
the home to loss and unending grief. The scents would kill anyone that has
the misfortune of encountering them.
But even the antiseptic is a liar. It's only here to tell you everything is
controlled and safe. It wants you to believe you'll be okay, your people will
be okay. But it can only hide the past. When the smell of rain begins
entering the seemingly sealed hospital room, the antiseptic cannot hide it.
When grief overtakes the heartbroken mother, when the brother punches a
hole in the wall because someone must hold back their tears, and when the
little baby isn't placed in its mother's arms after birth, the antiseptic can only
wait at the door till it has passed. Till the halls are empty once more. Only
then can it hide the reality of death.

title: The Price of Prejudice is the Same as Your Perfume
author: Paravin
excerpt: Your designer perfume covers the metallic, disgustingly rich scent of blood.
imageAlt: Cover image for The Price of Prejudice is the Same as Your Perfume
content: Your designer perfume covers the metallic, disgustingly rich scent of blood.
What exactly are refugee camps supposed to be? Hope, relief and maybe
even joy. Babies held by their mothers who lovingly hum melodies lost to
war, children fly kites, running around to fly theirs higher. The reality of
these camps cast a horrifying shadow over these expectations. There is
never enough. Enough food, water, beds, tents for anyone. These
refugees, they do not live, but they are not dead. They are the line between
life and death. Refugee camps are operated under bureaucratic systems.
Identity is ripped away and disposed of. Names are replaced with
designated numbers. You are not a person, you are a figure.
You must be grateful you're alive, nothing else. Hope? Joy? How can these
even cross the minds of the unfortunate souls tied down to these places
when their lives have been stripped down to the barest form- survival. Joy
is but a distant memory that moves away farther and farther for each day of
fight for those who wake simply to survive. Refugee camps are not home to
hope and wishes for a better new day, they're akin run down shops by the
beach selling lifeless shells, once considered human.
Refugee camps, concentration camps and warzones are necropolitical
structures. Necropolitics refers to a socio-political use of power to impose
decisions on who may live or die. These structures are referred to as
“death worlds”, because that is unequivocally what they are. People are
subject to such harsh, unimaginable conditions that living seems but a
distant memory, something that happened but can no longer. Lives are lost
before the light has ceased. And nobody bats an eye. Because death
worlds are grey zones where death is the standard.
These structures exist due to dehumanization. Those in power justify their
actions as in their eyes, the damned are damn bugs. Insects that are
simple inconveniences to be disposed of. While to the public, they are
outsiders. Refugees are “those” people. Whatever happens to “them” are
outside events. We believe such things will never happen to us, because,
well, we aren't them. We are made to believe we are somehow different
from them. Everything based around these people, these structures, work
to separate.
The linguistics of these areas also lighten their reality. When told someone
died yesterday, the regular person shakes their head and moves on. But
when told that a mother of two was murdered yesterday over something
completely trivial, it brings out more of a visceral reaction. This is the exact
tactic used to cover up the reality of these areas. Alongside the classic
necropolitical tactic of indirect death, i.e., creating circumstances where
survival is the least plausible outcome, then treating the effects of those
circumstances as something uncontrollable, allowing those in power to
dodge accountability seamlessly. Countless people lose their lives due to
‘unforeseen circumstances’, while in reality, they’ve been killed, indirectly or
even directly. But the public is only told a number of people passed away at
a camp. We are not told about the mother who escaped war with her child
to find any kind of help, or the innocent bystander who got abducted and
imprisoned because of his beliefs. So, we never question it. We let it
continue. Dehumanization is a shape shifting creature, acting as a noose
for the condemned and a blindfold for the privileged.
We are only able to see them in such a dimmed light of humanity because
of the slow but steady eradication of empathy in modern society. Its
disappearance is no simple matter of times changing, it is a play
orchestrated by the same composers that create the melody of war with the
sound of military drones and gunfire. We are taught to feel for those who
look like us, those who believe in the same things as us, speak the same
language as us. Everyone is told it does not matter because it is not
happening to them or their people, so they have nothing to worry about.
“No need to feel empathetic for someone you don't even know!” This
rhetoric is so powerful because it breeds a complacent society while
ensuring those who speak out look out of place.
People consumed by this mindset execute every excuse with near-perfect
apathy to justify it. They will never know; the more they ignore the suffering
of people they do not relate to, the closer they themselves get to
oppression. Who will protect them when their people are next? The people
who ingrained this mindset in the masses will never teach them the
consequences of it. After all, they are the ones benefiting from it. We as a
society are designed to never even think of the possibility that one day it
may be ‘our’ people. As a divided and complacent society is the end goal
for the power consumed entities, the general public never considering the
possibility of being victimized is a step in the right direction.  How could
they ever know the truth? Groomed to ignore, forced to never look past
what is shown.
The form of empathy that is taught to the public at present adds to this. It is
nothing but a repackaged form of prejudice. You can feel empathetic for
your people, but not those people. It's perfect for those who set up this
system of apathy and ignorance. They are the only ones winning from it.
Separation will never save us.
The scent of bloodshed will never reach the ones responsible for it, though
it leaks in through their front door, they can afford to cover the smell with
overpriced cologne and burnt cigars. Everyone else will be outside,
wondering if they had acknowledged and protected the condemned, would
things have turned out differently? Necropolitics will only exempt a person
as long as they can afford the privilege to turn a blind eye to reality. When
ignorance continues winning, who will be the next statistic?

title: "He is SO babygirl!!!!!" The Rebrand of Gender Norms
author: Paravin
excerpt: Society still believes boys like blue and girls like pink
imageAlt: Cover image for "He is SO babygirl!!!!!" The Rebrand of Gender Norms
content: Society still believes boys like blue and girls like pink
Not the way you think. If one were to say this phrase aloud, they would be
made the subject of a hearty laugh. Now, girls can do things traditionally
associated with boys and vice versa. But it wasn't always like this. Blue,
Video games, skateboarding, anything deemed “masculine” was obviously
for boys. Pink, flowers, makeup, gossiping; they're all “feminine” things.
Liking something associated with the opposite gender would make you the
perfect target for ridicule. “Ew, are you a boy or something?” Or “why are
you acting like a girl? Man up.”
We like to believe we've grown past that. Past words like “feminine” and
“masculine” that don't actually mean anything. And to an extent, we are.
But we haven't eradicated gender norms, not even close. They've now
evolved to sound socially aware and as if they're actually breaking gender
norms.
Let's see some examples. Anyone who's been on the internet has seen the
term “malewife” or heard the phrase “she's the man”. “Malewife” is a term
associated with men who seem to be more meek, fragile or gentle. While
the latter phrase describes a woman who's strong, often rough and has a
strong work ethic. Again, there has been a trend of calling men who have
longer hair, softer features or demeanors wives or girlfriends, and women
with short hair and less soft demeanors are husband material.  Because as
we know, wives and girlfriends are weak, fragile and porcelain dolls that
must be protected, while husbands and boyfriends  are strong and work
driven. Isn't that what we all believe in? That women and men have certain
traits completely original to their respective genders?
We don't directly say that long hair is feminine or that short hair is
masculine, we make sure to twist the roles to hide what we're ashamed of.
The shameful truth that gender roles have gone absolutely nowhere.
They're as clear and horrible as they've always been.
Because frankly, they're harmful to a degree that's hard to explain. They
perpetuate what's already wrong with society, while making the receiver
feel uncomfortable in who they are. Obviously there's nothing wrong with
being a man or woman, but many are not comfortable with being called the
opposite gender in such a patronizing manner. It's not outright
dehumanizing, but it leaves a strange lingering feeling of not belonging.
Gender dysphoria is thriving from our brand new flavour of stereotypes.
I believe it started from fictional characters. Because people justify
perpetuating gender stereotypes when it's towards fictional characters
because they're not even real, it's not that serious. Until people feel
comfortable speaking that way about real people. We deny how much our
interactions with fiction carry into real life. Because it would challenge our
beliefs and we would have to actually change how we behave; oh, the
horror. Fictional characters do not have feelings. People do. Parasocialism
allows us to push the boundaries of people until it reaches a tipping point,
then those same people are demonized for speaking up about how they
feel. Because we have become so comfortable in these anti reversed
gender roles that speaking up against them seems to be the harmful
choice. Fiction allows people to justify certain actions and advertise them.
Gender norms have gone nowhere. Society still believes in “femininity” and
“masculinity”. And we will for a long time coming. At the end of the day, that
man with slightly long hair is not your girlfriend, it's a grown man.

title: i gave my nana the raincoat
author: Zahraa Zee
excerpt: To: mijanur.rahman1243@yahoo.com
imageAlt: Cover image for i gave my nana the raincoat
content: To: mijanur.rahman1243@yahoo.com
Subject: hi

okay so i know this goes nowhere. i know. the account is probably dead or it isn't dead which is worse. it's just sitting there with 14000 unread and mine goes in with the loan offers and the discount codes and the ones that say your package is waiting, like my grief is a promotional offer, like it will sit in a folder called junk which is, honestly, the most accurate folder anyone has ever named anything, and nobody will ever open it because the person who had the password is the person i am writing to, and i knew all that before i opened this and i opened it anyway at 1am on a tuesday so draw your own conclusions about me.
i gave you the raincoat.
that's it. that's the email. i stop here every time.

i gave you the raincoat because i wanted the umbrella. it was red and it was pretty and it had some cartoon on it that i can't even name now, that's how much it mattered, and the only thing that mattered was that it was MINE, nana, it was mine and i wanted to carry it, the way a child wants something, which is not really wanting, it's closer to needing, there's no gap in it to put a reason into. and ma put the raincoat in your hands and said put it on her and you looked at me — and i said no. you said nothing! you just put it on, the transparent polythene one, the coral pink one you could see straight through, and you walked me home in it, a grown man in a child's rain cover, and i have thought about how you must have looked maybe four hundred times and i still cannot let myself see it properly, my brain goes blurry at the edges like it's protecting me, and i don't want to be protected, i want to see it, i want to see exactly how stupid you looked carrying my dignity for me.

and then i FELL. i fell. in the mud, in the brown water that looks two inches deep and is not, i sat down in it like a dropped bag and my socks filled up and i cried, not because it hurt, i need you to know it did not hurt, i cried because i was embarrassed and because the water was cold and because i already knew who i was going to blame
and i blamed you.

i went home and i told ma i fell and i let her fill in the rest and she filled it in the way i wanted her to, she yelled at you, her own father, in the living room, in front of me, and i stood there in my brown uniform with mud going up my spine like a ladder and i did not say one word. one word. "i gave him the raincoat." nine syllables. five seconds. i had them. i didn't spend them. and you didn't say it either, that's the part i can't get past, you had the whole truth in your mouth and you swallowed it to keep me clean, you let her think you were careless with me when you have never been careless with me once, not one time, not ever, and you just stood there with your head bowed and took it, your head was BOWED, nana, you bowed your head for something i did, and then it was over and i went and changed my clothes.

why did i do that. why did i do that. i've been asking for five years and the answer is just "you were nine" and that answer is true and it does NOTHING, it does nothing, it's like being handed a receipt for something you can't return
sorry. i'm sorry. i don't know who i'm apologising to, you can't read this, this is going to junk

the lychees. you peeled them with your thumbnail so my hands wouldn't get sticky. you bought six dal puri and ate one so i wouldn't be eating alone and i only worked that out this year, i worked that out at SIXTEEN, i was eating next to a man's kindness for years and i thought it was just how puri came. the salted chips in the silver packet that cut the roof of my mouth. the clemon sweating in the glass. the sticker sheets for absolutely no reason, no birthday, no result, no nothing, just a man handing a child stickers. pencils. colour pencils. the cloth doll that one birthday with the stitched eyes and the soft body, and i was so happy with it, that's the thing, i was happy, i loved it and i loved you, i was never once ungrateful, i knew exactly what i had, and that is precisely what i cannot explain, because how do you love someone that much and take that much from their hands and still never once say sorry. how did i do that. i had years. he was right there for years. and i never said it, not because i didn't feel it, i felt it the whole time, i just kept not saying it, like it was a thing i could do later, like he was a permanent arrangement

and then 2021. the front room. the katha laid over your body, the one sewn out of squares of other cloth, the one that was made out of scraps — nanu's old salwars, frayed pillow covers, old blankets — everything that was left over, and i noticed it and i still see those squares when i close my eyes.

and i cried. i cried so hard. i sat down at your feet and i cried like something was being pulled out of me, baba had to come and hold me and talk me down and i couldn't stop, because it had just arrived, the whole thing had just arrived at once, that it was FOREVER, that there was no later anymore, that every sorry i was saving had just become permanently unspendable, and that i never told you i loved you, i never said the sentence, i thought it constantly and i never once said it out loud to your face and now the face was under a quilt
your feet.
i was AT your feet. i was sitting right there at them. and even then i didn't take them in my hands.

they were cracked at the heel. white lines in them like dried earth, from sandals, from hot roads, from walking to my school and back twice a day for years for a child who wanted to hold her own red umbrella. we do that in this family, we hold each other's feet, it costs nothing, and i had sixteen hundred chances and i used zero of them, and the one time i finally sat down at your feet you couldn't feel it

i can't fix it. that's- that's the whole thing. there's no version where i get to go back and hand you the raincoat and take the yelling and press my thumbs into your heels and say sorry and say the other thing, the i love you nana, the four words i was sitting on like an egg. the guilt isn't a visitor anymore, it moved in, it pays no rent...

i carry an umbrella with me whenever i go outside (and a book, i love books nana, i know you would love to hear me speak of them). i always lend it to others, friends, strangers at gates, my sisters, before i've even decided to. i used to think that was kindness and it isn't. i am so spontaneous now nana. i hardly think before i speak, the words cascade over my lips and pool at my feet and i think i have learned this because i will never get a second chance. because
i hope you're cool under there. i hope there is soft grass cushioning your feet.
thank you for being the best nana in the world.
ok. sending it. to junk. whatever. i love you, i love you, i'm so sorry, i miss you so much it hits me at 3am and leaves me with hot, swollen eyes.
your zaara-moni
Glossary
nana — maternal grandfather, the mother's father
nanu — maternal grandmother
ma — mother
baba — father
katha — a quilt stitched at home from layers of worn-out cloth and scraps
salwar — loose trousers worn under a long tunic
dal puri — a small flatbread stuffed with spiced lentils and fried
Clemon — a Bangladeshi lemon soft drink-moni — a suffix of endearment attached to a name; moni means gem

content: you stand under the mistletoe
and i under vines of bougainvillea
your breath of snow against my rain soaked palms
mulled wine spilling where my tea leaves drown
bells echo in your chapels
mine rings with rickshaw pullers
your streets polished like clear glass
mine cracked open with tire marks
gardens of ivy whisper through your fences
cicadas hum inside my chest
rose hedges heavy over your gates
mine dusted with mango skins and marigold
your snowdrops lie pressed flat in books
my jasmine goes brown before morning
your apples keep all winter in the cellar
my lychees spoil inside a week
you taste of buttered bread
i of chilies crushed on stone
my tamarind arrives at your table in sugar
my dried fish does not arrive at all
yet the same moon
drifts between us
silver trembling
whole in your window
and in my two wet hands
breaking
and breaking
and still
mine.
