By Tahsina Tabassum Writi
Yay Almighty, I pray you to be my God
My God doesn’t stop me while I cry
And doesn’t order me to praise him at my lowest
He orders me feel my pain gracefully,
So he can feel with me too
He said, “Overcome your sufferings with me
Grow with me
I have build myself all my own
I can help you build you too
I have grown alone enough
Now you experience me to grow
Let me share your suffering with me
Let us grow together "
My God can do miracles
And doesn’t ask if I have prayed or not
My God doesn't limit human with boundaries
We are his favorite creation
I asked," What if I suppress you"
He said," You can’t, I can grow all my own
But you will need my help
And if you do
Then I can build myself powerful again
I don't fear that anyone will suppress me
I am building myself every moment
I can build you too"
My God doesn’t want servants
Who don’t understand him
Who can't love him
He said, " Your happiness is not separated from me, nor your pain is
I can feel you while laughing while crying
I hope you can feel me too"
I challenge you to be as powerful,
as kind, and as pure as my God
I will surrender my everything to love you

title: Catastrophize
author: Zohara H. Khan
excerpt: Baba’s Silence
imageAlt: Cover image for Catastrophize
content: Catastrophize
Baba’s Silence

“Hama amada hastand? (Is everyone ready?)” Baba’s voice echoed inside our silent house, his eyes never meeting ours as we nodded, before he began walking out with the rest of us following behind like ducklings following their mother duck.

Our little journey to the cars awaiting us outside was eerily silent, with just the sound of our burkas swishing with the movement of our legs while I clasped my gloved hands in front of me. My sisters, their husbands, and my brother held equal expressions before we finally made it to the cars that will take us to our ancestral home in Istalif.

Baba was on the front seat with the driver, with Jawad, my brother, my third and fourth sister, Laila and Nilab, and I on the back, our emotions shrouded behind our niqabs. In the second car was my eldest sister Marzia, her husband Hamid and my second sister Soraya, with her husband Farid. Hamid and Farid never really got along, so I cannot say how awkward that ride must have been. I mean, my own ride was awkward enough, with not a single word exchanged. Or was it a peaceful silence in disguise?
There was a third vehicle trailing behind us, silently, all alone, but a part of us nonetheless. Nobody inside my car spoke a word about it.

The city of Kabul passed by us in the blink of an eye, until we were surrounded by lush greenery, followed by mountainous terrains. Not long after that, the roads began to look familiar, livelier, as villages came to view and I knew we had made it to Istalif. And soon, we’d make it to our ancestral home, where I’d finally have to face my reality. The reality I’m trying so hard to avoid.

Someone in the car sniffled, I couldn’t say who, and I didn’t want to find out either. Comforting each other was pointless, for there was no comfort to be found anywhere at the moment. Speaking would only make me confront the reality, and the reality would make me do more than just sniffle, and I didn’t want to do that just yet. For the little time I have been given to myself, I wish to spend it in quietness, without thinking about where I’m headed.

At long last, the cars came to a stop, but not without being greeted by a series of faces of men I quickly recognized as my uncles and cousin brothers, all holding solemn expressions as they made way for me and my sisters to be let out.

Like a puppet, I followed my sisters’ movements and went wherever they did, but I could not bring myself to lift my head and look up at whatever everyone else was looking as the third vehicle rounded the corner and came to a stop before everyone’s eyes, and there it was. The bier.

The sniffles got louder among the ladies, but quiet enough not to anger the men as they all gathered around the bier to lift it up and place it inside our house, where my maman will receive her final goodbyes from the family she had known for more than fifty years.

Yet, I could not bring myself to lift my head, even as my maman, now wrapped inside a kafan and held up by the bier, was placed in her living room that she had decorated herself years ago. As the scent of incense took over the whole area and people began excusing themselves to give us, her children and husband, a minute.
Yet, I could not lift my head.
I could not, for the life of me, still accept that maman, whose warm hands I held not even twenty-four hours ago, was now cold as ice. I did not even want to think of it.
I did not want to believe maman could die.
Why Maman?

Ever since my family moved back to Afghanistan from the UAE, there has not been a single winter in our lives when we didn’t have to visit the hospital. It was always one thing or the other, and it always concerned maman.

Starting from the winter of 2013, when she had her first brain stroke, not to forget the menopause and the toll it took on her already depraved health. Barely conscious, paralyzed, and sanity halfway gone, I believe part of her had already died back then.

The following winter was spent making sure we didn’t have a repeat of the previous one. Then came 2015, and we must have cut some slack, because then started her seizures, body convulsing like a fish out of water. It was scary, as if she was possessed, with her mouth foaming and eyes rolling backwards. The doctors later said she had epilepsy. Another added to the list.

There was no time to take precaution for the winter of 2016, for a surprise was already awaiting us. Maman was maman alright, but her body had started a new dance of trembling from head to toe- literally. Her speech was more disoriented, and she could barely hold an object without including it in her dance moves. We were later told she had Parkinson's.

Did peace return to us after that? Probably, if one can call it that. With the threat of dementia slowly taking over our maman day by day, we spent the next few winters in a strange bliss, ignorant bliss, perhaps. Marzia got married in the winter of 2018, which might have been the happiest winter we’ve had since coming back to Afghanistan. Then came 2020. Covid.

Not to worry, maman did not get diagnosed with that. We made sure she was protected to the best of our abilities. But unfortunately for us, we forgot to protect her from the rest of the demons lurking in the shadows.

When we rushed her to the hospital this time, we were told she had only three days left to live. Fifteen days for the GBS to take over the organs and shut them down, and it was day twelve already. Her whole body was paralyzed. The only thing functioning was her heart and head.
Lucky for us there was a cure, and it could still be administered before the fifteen days are up. It sure cost us a fortune, but we were willing to take our chances, no matter how slim it may be.
Maman, once again, beat the odds and survived. Recovery took months, almost a year, but she was alive and living, that was all that mattered.

2022 came and Soraya got married. This wedding wasn’t very fun, for like every winter, it was spent worrying over mothers declining health, and this time she could not make it to her daughter’s wedding even.

2023, and she was looking so much better than ever before, to the point she made a grand entrance to Laila’s wedding. It seemed like good fortune was smiling down at us in those years, for she was well enough to see through not only Nilab’s wedding as well, but also her first grandchild, Marzia’s daughter.
The heavens were really smiling down at us, only to hide their evil smirk behind.
Because it so happened that Nilab was the only one who didn’t marry during winter, so the winter of 2025 was still to be accounted for. And when it did arrive, it came bearing gifts.
Not only was maman diagnosed with severe pneumonia with risk of damaged lungs, but was also septic from the hospital ICU. Chances of survival were slim.
Fate is a funny thing. How it always expected maman to withstand all of this was beyond me. Maman was no wonder woman, how much more did they expect from her? How long could she take it?

But I must have misunderstood her, for once again, maman defied all odds and survived. Once more, she made it back to us. Fate threw all the turd it could find at maman and she still chose to return to us, which was why I always believed she would come back to us, no matter what. That nothing could bring maman down, and we had a lot of time in our hands.
She was still to see me and Jawad get married after all.

So when I held her warm hands with my own and felt her delicate skin against mine, I did not know it would be the last time they’d ever be this warm. That the ever-aging hands of maman would suddenly turn ice cold, and hard as stone only seven hours after that.
And the funniest part, this is me only guessing. I do not know whether she really is cold and hard as I say, for I still haven’t touched a part of her. It is only what I’m told dead people feel like.

My aunts made their way one by one, gently pried the kafan from her face to expose it and laid gentle kisses on her forehead in a silent farewell. I knew they were crying, I could hear them in the silence, but any noise louder than that and things could get ugly.

The people poured in like rushing water, some even coming to pat us on our heads and offer chaste kisses on our cheeks, but I was too out of it to address them. They didn’t mind. I was bereaved after all.

My sisters were now starting to talk, deciding on which guests to greet, and when it would be our turn to bid farewell. Some of our closest female cousins were huddled around them, offering support when it came to greeting the more unfamiliar faces. My sisters were handling it fairly better than me. Why?
Was it because they already had families after marrying? Another mother to always turn to? Children to look forward to? A husband to lean on?
Then what of me? Who do I turn to?
The only family I have is this. The only mother I had was maman. So, who will I go crying to?
I’m not even married yet. Maman never got to see me marry. Why…

Baba and Jawad made their way inside the room, and instantly the hubbub disappeared. It was only then did I finally lift my head up and look at them, at anyone at all. My face, veiled under the niqab, was evidently bone dry, unlike my sisters.  I was still to shed a single tear.
Baba’s face was moist just like the rest of them, eyes bloodshot as he fidgeted with his cuffs before turning to all his daughters.
“Waqt ast.”
It is time.
Color of Death

The bile stuck in my throat suddenly felt like it was turning to lead, making it harder for me to swallow as my sisters all got to their feet at once, expecting me to do the same. Like the puppet I was, I did, albeit in shaky legs, for I knew what was to come next. I had seen what happened next in kaka Ibrahim's funeral.

The first to break down in a fit of tears was Marzia herself, for she had always been the louder one among all when it came to crying. Hamid had rushed to her in an attempt to lower her voice so the elderly wouldn’t frown at her, making Farid rush to Soraya too although his wife was much quieter than Marzia. Cousin Bushra held Laila as she cried her heart out, her niqab sticking to her face as she glanced at maman before burying her face in Bushra’s shoulder. Jawad stood beside Nilab and patted her on the shoulder with one hand in order to calm her whimpers while also wiping his own tears on the side.
They were all expressing their grief at the loss of their mother. It was the most normal thing to do. So why was I yet to shed a tear?

“Roya.” I heard maman’s voice in my head, the last time she ever called my name as she gently grabbed my hands in her soft warm ones, smiling at me as her eyes turned to crescents. “Biya pesh az in-ke meyla basta shawa, yak bar-e diga berem, janam? (Let’s go to the fair once more before it closes, alright?)”

I grin plastered on my face, her suggestion making me giddy all over knowing how against she was about going to the fair before until we had forced her to come. For the first time in years, maman had seen the outside world without the hospital windows and it’s safe to say, she loved it. I eagerly nodded, placing my hands on top of hers. “Chera ke na? Waqti Soraya bargasht, yak bar-e diga merem. (I don’t see why not? Let us go again when Soraya returns.)”

“Bale! Bale, hatman merawim! (Yes! Yes, we will!)” Maman agreed like a child. “Wa in bar metanem Jawad ra ham ba khod bebarim, Farzana ra ham. Motma'en hastam ke u ham khosh meshawa ba Jawad yakja biyaya. (And we can also take Jawad with us this time, and Farzana as well. I’m sure she’d love to come along with Jawad.)”

My smile faltered at the name, but I held my ground and agreed, despite knowing all too well that the woman named Farzana would never join. For she was not even real to begin with. She was someone maman had created in her own mind.
Have I mentioned that maman’s memory has been failing more and more lately due to dementia? Oftentimes, it was hard for her to even recognize us.
“Albata. (Of course.)” I forced my smile to stay. “Farzāna ham bā mā meyāya. (Farzana will come along too.)”
Someone must have pulled maman’s hand out of the kafan, because now it was out on display, and that was the first thing I noticed the moment I decided to look up.
Maman’s hand, once a warm beige, now a pale grey. Like the color of death.
And then, the first drop of tear fell.
The Windows of the Soul

I remember kaka Ibrahim’s funeral. Baba, Jawad, Laila and I were the only ones who could go. Baba was devastated, for it was his oldest brother and the one who adored him the most. Kaka Ibrahim was a kind soul indeed, he was the only one who made this place feel like home since we returned to Afghanistan. Now he was gone, and his home felt like a distant memory of the past.

Laila and I had gone with his daughter’s-in-law to bid him farewell, and behind us was his wife and two sisters. They cried like they had never cried before, howling so loud I feared the men would come barging in. But nobody did. It was Kaka Ibrahim’s family after all.

Laila was crying too, holding on to kaka Ibrahim’s granddaughter as she too bawled her eyes out. I too was crying, but I could not bring myself to be loud, I barely interacted with him. Yes, he was a great man, good to my family, and baba loved him a lot. I spied baba through the door watching Laila and me, and that was what made me tear up, seeing baba cry like a little boy for his brother.
Kaka Ibrahim didn’t look anything like himself.
They say the soul defines most of our appearance, and perhaps it was because the body no longer had a soul, kaka Ibrahim looked unrecognizable.
Maman must look beyond unrecognizable too.
I remember her chubby cheeks, her lopsided smile that I inherited. The way her eyes would crinkle when she chuckled, or how her once stubby hands turned wrinkly not with age, but with illnesses.
Her hands.
They were unrecognizable.

“M-Mam… maman.” The first word of the day had finally slipped my lips, barely audible, but out nonetheless. My sisters were calling out to her more and more, as if begging her to wake up and come back to them, only that she never did. Maman never came back.
She was dead.
My maman… was dead. And I only shed a tear.
Was it because I was still to come to terms with my reality? That maman was indeed gone? Is that why I couldn’t even bring myself to help in washing her body when my sisters did it just fine?
Were they fine?

With trembling lips and eyes burning with unshed tears, I finally willed myself to do that one thing I had not done in the last seven hours. I had not looked at maman’s face even once, even when I had refused to help in washing her body. Too scared of what I would find, or how it would feel to touch her, I ran away, leaving my sisters to complete the task.
I could not bring myself to look at a version of her that will never look back at me again.
But goodbyes only come once, and sometimes don’t come at all. Only the fortunate get to say goodbye. Should I count myself fortunate to get a chance to see my maman’s dead face?

Someone held back a moan, a male, and instantly, my eyes shot up, only to find baba, once again, crying to himself silently, just like the day kaka Ibrahim had died. Only this time he wasn’t a little boy, but a husband that lost his wife.
Baba, the strongest figure I know, cried his heart out as he stared at his wife’s face. Maman’s face.
And as if that was the push I needed, I too did the same.
I did not wait to brace myself, or tell myself I didn’t need to. Before I knew it, I was already looking at her, and oh… I was right.
Maman was unrecognizable.
Gaunt cheeks replaced her chubby ones, mouth slightly parted in a final sigh. hairs pushed back to expose her full face and her eyes, her pretty chocolate brown eyes…
I could not see them. They were hidden behind the veil of death.

“Maman.” I whispered, and all too suddenly, it seemed like the body was coming to life. As if I had just spoken the magic word, and the body on the bier was becoming the maman of my memories. The maman I knew.

“Maman?” Like a fool, or like a child lost, I called out for my mother, eyes stinging with tears as the second drop fell and then the third, while my trembling hands lifted up to hover over her own cold once. Those warm hands that held mine not long ago, making me promise about the fair.
Will they still be that warm?
My fingers closed around her own, and I flinched.
It was ice cold.
Maman was dead. Right before me.
Death’s Embrace

Why did nobody ever tell me that goodbyes were this painful? Is it because it cannot be described in words? Is that why I cannot put into words as to what it feels like holding my mother’s ice-cold hand in mine?

With trembling hands, I lift her hand up to my veiled cheeks, trying to feel anything at all, only to come out empty handed. It’s hard and stiff like cardboard, but the wrinkles say this is maman no doubt.

I want to ask her to wake up like Marzia is doing, howl and cry like madar kalan is doing as she feigns to miss her daughter, but my voice seems to fail me. All I can do is whimper like a lost kitten, hold on to her hand as it gets heavier in mine and repeat one word over and over again.
“Maman. M-maman…”

It’s getting harder to speak with the never ending bile stuck to my throat, and the burning in my eyes as the unshed tears finally spill out, first once, then twice, then thrice, until I lose count. I’m finally crying, finally mourning my mother, and I do not even know what to say.
What should I say? That I miss her? That I wish she was still here? Will she hear me?

All around me is my family tearing their hearts out at the loss before us, the noises so loud one could go deaf, but everything feels like a distant siren to me. Like I’m under water. No one, but just maman and me in our own world.
When holding onto her hand gets exhausting, I reach for her gaunt face, brushing a trembling finger over her concrete like face which makes me sob even harder, knowing how much she’d hate this.
Maman always took care of her skin. She always had a Glow & Lovely cream that she applied, and when Marzia married, she brought her a better Nivea moisturizer. She’d hate her skin like this.
“Oh maman…” I wailed despite myself unable to hold myself back anymore as I buried my face in her chest and let it all out.
What do I do now? How do I live in a world where maman is no more?
She will never see me married, never see my children, never get to travel like we promised her. She had only started enjoying the little joys in life, and now she was gone.
What could I do now!?

“MAMAN!” I felt hands nudging me to let her go, trying to pry me off of her but I could not do so yet. I could not let go. I could not let her be buried under all that soil. Maman still had so much to see. I still had so much time to spend with maman. Why must I lose her so?

“Roya. Roya!” My siblings were hugging me now, in an attempt to pry me off as we cried our hearts together. Someone must have pulled the kafan over maman’s face, because now I no longer could see it, and that sent me in a panic mode.
“Maman! Maman!”

But my cries fell to deaf ears, because soon, the bier was lifted, and baba, Jawad, Hamid, Farid, and the rest of the men took my mother away from her home one last time, to put her to her final resting place. And all I could do was wonder one thing as the sorrow began to settle in.
What will I do if maman ever dies like this?
The Voice in My Head

“M-Maman…” My wails were slowly turning to whimpers the moment the realization dawned on me that the bier was long gone from the room. It was time for me to come back to reality, but oh did it hurt so much.

The idea of me never being able to see maman smile despite all her illnesses again was like the fires of Jahannam for me. Which was all the more reason I should be pulling myself together now. I must.

I tried to compose my breathing, but the tears that began flowing would just not stop. My eyes were still closed in denial, the last scene being that of maman in the bier, resting in her living room one last time.
That image needed to go.

“…Wa baʿdesh, ba Jawad megoyam az Farzana beporsa ke u ham mekhaya ba ma biyaya ya na. Ya fekr mekoni khodam azash beporsam? Roya jan? (…and then, I will ask Jawad to ask Farzana if she would like to come too. Or do you think I should ask her myself? Roya?)”
My breathing was still erratic, hands still trembling, but the images before my eyes were now turning into a blur, as if dissolving.
“Roya? Roya jan, bacham, chera inqadr gerya mekoni? (Roya? Roya, my child, what has you crying so?)”

As soon as the voice registered itself in my mind, the images of my ancestral home living room were gone, and so was the nauseous scent of incense. The hubbub had died down too, replaced by a sheer sense of peaceful silence, the scent of warm sunlight wafting around me. And the next time I opened my eyes, my surroundings were completely different, but not unfamiliar.
I was home. Back in Kabul.
With maman.

“Roya.” The warmth of her hand in mine began to course through me all over again, as if she was breathing life into me anew. As if I was the one coming back from death. But nobody had died to begin with. Maman was right here, right before me.
“Gerya nakon, bachem. Hama-chi jor mesha. (Don’t you cry, my child. It will be alright.)”

A gasp escaped my lips, like someone had pulled me out of water and filled my lungs with air again, realization dawning on me over what I had done. Or what I was doing. Crying my heart out over something I had created on my own, by myself, in my head. A figment of my imagination.
But it felt… so real, maman’s death felt… so inevitable.
What was I thinking?
“Hama-chi jor mesha. Dafʿa-ye baʿd ke ba meyla raftem, har chi khasti barat mekharam, ha? (It will be alright. I shall buy you whatever you ask the next time we go to the fair, hmm?)”
Maman’s aging hands reached out to wipe the tears I had shed over the idea of her eminent end, one that has never even happened yet, but felt so real in my head.

Perhaps, everything will be alright indeed. It will be. The tragedy I imagined just now is nothing but just what I said- imagination. Maman was not going anywhere anytime soon. There won’t be any funeral in the next seven hours. I was just… catastrophizing.
And I cannot even help it.

Maman may be alive, but every day her survival hangs by a thread. Every day is a walk on eggshells, a ticking time bomb as we wait with our breaths caught in our lungs as we wonder and wait for something… anything out of order to happen. Every day is a survival game for us.
Because nobody knows when will be the last day maman smiles at us as she’s doing now.
For this once, I did not want to tell her that Farzana wasn’t real, and that she was all in her head. Not that I didn’t want to, I could not.
I sniffled, pulling my tears back while leaning into her touch with a smile. “Har tor ke shomā bekhāhin, māmān jān. (As you wish, maman.)”

For even if maman is alive and well now, our minds have already begun preparing us for the worst that we cannot bring ourselves to face. Our minds are catastrophizing in their own way, showing us what it’d feel like if the inevitable comes to pass.
But the real question is, do I even want to prepare myself for it?
Does preparing me for the loss actually protect me from the grief it brings?
THE END

title: The Commercialisation of Education in Bangladesh
author: Syrirah
excerpt: The Commercialisation of Education
imageAlt: Cover image for The Commercialisation of Education in Bangladesh
content: The Commercialisation of Education
in Bangladesh
In recent years, many coaching and admission centres have popped up all over
Bangladesh for students of all grades. Parents nowadays hope to get their children ahead of
the syllabus and readily enrol them in these centres, and many students also aim to get into
the best batches or courses possible. What does this commercialisation of education and
coaching culture tell us about our education system, and is its impact on the system and its
future positive or negative?
This culture has embedded itself into our academic lifestyle for various reasons. It is
an open secret that the quality of Bangladesh's education system is not the best. We may be
producing some excellent scientists, doctors and engineers through our universities, but the
quality of education in many of our schools and colleges is lacking. This leaves many
students feeling that their time in class is wasted and that they would learn better at home or
at a coaching centre, so they end up enrolling in the physical or online courses these centres
offer. Unfortunate as it is, we must admit, with some shame, that more often than not the
courses at these centres help students understand the material better than their schools or
colleges do.
Additionally, many parents in our country have an extremely harmful habit of treating
education and marks as a competition. This is somewhat justified given our education
system and job sector, and the mentality is prevalent in many Asian countries, but it has also
made its way into Bangladesh. It may stem from the fact that many parents of the millennial
and Gen Z generations did not have as fortunate a childhood or youth as we do, and did not
have as many opportunities to do things freely. They have seen, and are aware of, the
"survival of the fittest" system of our country, and they hope to set us up for success by
ingraining that mentality in us. Nonetheless, they forget that the main purpose of education is
to teach us not only academics but also morals, manners and values, among other things.
Our education system is partly to blame for that as well.
These coaching centres and courses do help many students who cannot understand
their material properly because of a lack of study material or other reasons, and they give
students exam practice they would otherwise not get. But they have also created a
reluctance to attend school and college, which seem useless when coaching centres and
one-shot courses can teach better and prepare students more effectively for school, college
and board exams. Although there is some truth to this, by focusing only on exams students
forget that schools and colleges are not just educational institutions. They also serve as
social hubs where students interact with people of different backgrounds and religions, and
as places to venture beyond the syllabus and take part in sports and extracurriculars.
Admittedly, many of our schools and colleges lack such an environment or such facilities.
The ever-increasing number of private coaching centres in our country shows how
much demand there is for them among students and parents. It also shows the failure of our
education system, which has made parents and students believe that the classes they
attend are not meaningful or helpful enough. Although coaching can help many students, in
many cases it may end up being a huge waste of time, money and potential, without the
students or their parents ever realising it.
Ultimately, these centres are having a negative impact on the mentality of our
students and parents, even if they are having a somewhat positive impact on students'
grades. I believe that if this system continues as it is, coaching centres and courses will
come to be seen as a replacement for our schools and colleges, which will become mere
places to register for board exams. The quality of our education system and curriculum must
be properly addressed, so that students no longer depend on coaching centres for their
education or for good marks, and need them only for additional or advanced study at best. If
we keep focusing only on marks, who will keep an eye on what we are actually learning, and
whether we are learning anything valuable at all?

title: I feel sorry for my dad
author: Sora
excerpt: For getting a daughter like me.
imageAlt: Cover image for I feel sorry for my dad
content: I feel sorry for my dad.
For getting a daughter like me.
He is like a Trojan,
never resting, always so consumed by his duties.
His day begins before the sun even rises.
The 24 hours I spend
resting, sleeping, eating
But to him, all of that is a luxury.
He is consumed by responsibilities,
a hectic life and constant worries.
Yet every day, when he gets home,
he never forgets to ask me about my day.
“Is there something you want to eat?”
My face lights up.
But despite all this,
I still feel sorry for him.
Sorry for the fact that I am his daughter.
A girl with no special qualities.
A girl who gets nervous so easily and messes everything up.
The one who tries to prove herself but fails.
Nothing but a wretched being.
Seeing him work so hard, do so much for me,
knowing that I'm just a good-for-nothing girl,
makes my heart ache.
He works so hard, but do I deserve his love?
I feel sorry for my dad.
Perhaps I should try to be a better daughter.

title: The Window
author: Tinkori
excerpt: Sometimes, It feels like life is bleeding through my fingers every other month
imageAlt: Cover image for The Window
content: Sometimes, It feels like life is bleeding through my fingers every other month
I float and dream of a time i will not have to be in my head for the moments I want to be real
But when reality knocks on my door and I see its long spindly shadow seep through the cracks
and darken my floors  I can sense it.
Like impending doom inside my ribcage
Like the putrid stench of lost dreams licking against my sinuses
Like the drum rolls of disappointment hammering against my senses.
I can see it   hear it   smell it
Taste it. Souring on my tongue and crawling toward the back of my throat to choke me
It does not want to kill me.
I wish it did.
It wants to trap me in my tower and strangle me just enough to leave me limping against the
limbo that is its true form.
Like a nightmare haunting my waking hours.
I consider retreating back to my bed.
To my laptop to my head to find something anything that will give me the high I need to slip out
of its shadowy fists crunching my bones beneath its illusive grip
I consider going to sleep.
I consider letting unconsciousness guide me through the days
The window blinks at me.
Patient. expectant. calling.
Flirting and flaunting in its stillness.
Blowing kisses to my pulse beating under the claustrophobic stretch of skin.
I look away first. Always first.
I consider opening the door.
Taking the gamble.
I will have to one day anyway.
I'm stuck in my spot in the hallway staring at its antlers swaying and still, growing and growing
until it reaches my toes like the growing tides of a full moon night.
It doesn't move further. Still stuck on the other side of my doorway.
Polite and sure.
Sure like the rising sun in the east sky that lightens my hallways and kitchen and the living room
and lightens the pulsating shadow lapping at my feet.
I retreat back into my bed for the day until it all begins again for the night.
eyes on my high for the day
Praying hoping that tonight it gets me up enough to let me forget about the ugliness of the
beauty I chase after through my books and dreams and notes and shows.
The window stays blinking at my back.
patient. expectant. stalling.
Flirting and flaunting in its stillness.
Blowing kisses at my beating heart,
throbbing under the dying stretch of muscles and bones that covers its miserable home
Still, expectant, patient, sure.
It's a long way down.

title: Bluest day
author: Advi
excerpt: Did your day go as planned?
imageAlt: Cover image for Bluest day
content: Did your day go as planned?
Was I ever included in your plan?
Did you feel the warmth in my hand?
Because I felt the blue
That lingered in yours.
Did my words penetrate your soul?
Because they crashed through mine.
Did you notice my flickering eyes,
Or were you too busy
Looking at the time?
Did you feel the spark of yellow
Burning somewhere in your blue,
Or was I the only one
Being consumed?
Is your blue sky so vast
That even when the sun makes it shine,
You forget that it exists?
I was wrapped in blue.
I was wrapped in you.
And so were you—
wrapped in blue,
wrapped in yourself.
You notice only yourself.
And somehow,
I notice only you.
Because I am yellow
And you are my blue.

title: Reach out
author: Advi
excerpt: Perhaps, the clay, God used to mould you was
imageAlt: Cover image for Reach out
content: Perhaps, the clay, God used to mould you was
blue,
perhaps the scraps left behind
were what He used to create my eyes.
For had it not been so,
I would never have known
how tenderly my Lord creates,
how meticulously He sculpts a poem,
how the poem He has breathed into existence
inspires a soul to write a thousand more.
My Lord has moulded you into a shade
beyond the comprehension of color,
beyond the reach of language,
beyond what words could ever hope to inscribe.
Perhaps He gathered you
from the vastness of a distant ocean.
For no matter how desperately I try to hold you,
you slip between my fingers,
leaving me drenched in your absence,
hollowed by the weight of what I cannot keep.
Perhaps He moulded you
from the breeze that wanders along the shore..
enough to send a shiver down my spine,
never enough to fill my lungs.
Enough to remind me that you exist,
never enough to let me breathe you in.
And yet, I know what He made you from.
From the creation He sculpted in haste,
from the eyes He, perhaps, had meant to color
differently,
from the very depths of my own gaze.
He made you from my eyes.
From my eyes.
From the liquid clay
that spilled forth whenever I wept.
He sculpted you from the tears of my loneliness,
from the salt of my longing,
from every silent prayer
that dried upon my lips.
He made you from me—
from the hollowed chambers of my being,
from the pieces of myself
I did not know I was losing.
And still, I sit and wonder—
How?
How can something born of me
belong to a world
that will never let me call it mine?
Just reach out your hand.
Place it against my heart.
Feel how it beats blue.
How it beats only for you.
it gasps your name with every ache,
whispers it through every fracture,
and breathes it into the silence
where your presence ought to be.
I pray for you
to the very One who made you,
to the One who blessed me
with this unbearable ache,
this exquisite torment
of loving what I cannot hold.
And now, all I can do
is pray for the longing to loosen its grip,
for this ceaseless ache to find its end—
for the final stillness
of that inevitable peace
we call death.

title: My blue
author: Advi
excerpt: Blue
imageAlt: Cover image for My blue
content: Blue
The blue I see isn't the blue you realize.
Perhaps it's the blue of the salted sea at
sunrise,
or the blue of a cold glass of water at 3 am
Maybe it's the blue outside your window
Or of the sky on a quiet spring afternoon.
Possibly it's in the sea when I go deep to
touch its ground
No—perhaps it's the blue that lingers
when you look away from the sun.
Even the feeling of sinking my hand into
rice
feels like your kind of blue.
I searched for you in my blue jeans,
but found nothing.
Perhaps I was looking too desperately.
You weren't in the blue-tinted windows of
my home.
But somehow, you were there
when I lay upon the dirt in early winter.
Maybe colorblindness is my only salvation
because the only color I have ever truly
seen
is blue.

title: Why?
author: Advi
excerpt: Why did you pull away so fast?
imageAlt: Cover image for Why?
content: Why did you pull away so fast?
Was the disgust so deep
you couldn't keep your hand in place?
Do you ever wonder what I felt?
To exist as the brightest thing
and yet remain the most unseen?
To feel like the sun
is to bear the cruelest fate—
to shine so brightly, to burn within,
while no one ever lifts their gaze.
You take my warmth.
You take my love.
You seek solace in me.
You turn to me when you need me.
But when I ask you to look at me,
you turn away—
Too bright. Too bright.
You tell me how your blue sky
has wrapped itself around me.
Was the bloom more beautiful than I?
Was it easier to notice
something that never asked
to be seen?
You asked about the bloom.
You never asked about me.
And yet—
You're in my head.
You're in my skin.
You're in my veins.
You're in my teeth.
You're in the coldest breaths I take,
in every sickness I survive.
“So I'm the peaceful kind.”
Oh, yes.
You are.
Your peace is indestructible.
And yet, somehow,
you destroy mine.
You're like the rain
that comes with autumn,
quiet and inevitable.
And I am the rainbow
left behind in a clear sky—
bright enough to be seen,
yet somehow
only good enough to spark
a passing interest.
Because you never needed me to exist.
And I couldn't even become
who I am
without you.
My dearest blue.

title: An Apology
author: Fahyaz A.
excerpt: It is rather strange, how our lives begin
imageAlt: Cover image for An Apology
content: An Apology
It is rather strange, how our lives begin
All crying, exposed, and unfurrowed skin.
There are many perhaps who should have known
Better. But brains were just as unfurrowed.
I was young then. Clutching my pen, penning
With great effort, emotions far too big
For that one muscle in my chest. Crying.
And in your eyes, I saw the reflection
Of the coward that disappointed both,
You and I. And I swore, I won't forget.
Or forgive. Yet time is a fickle thing.
My horns grew longer, my skin grew redder.
All the while, the cambion denied fault
For having tossed my soul in the shredder.
But I believed I could escape one day,
Or maybe I would understand someday.
The whys, and the whys, and the whys again
Why device wrinkles on unfurrowed skin?
And run away I did, once there's a way,
Unclenched the muscle, the first time that day.
Fleeing the burning pyre, I took a breath.
Infront of me, I saw that crying kid.
So, I raised him the way I wish I was,
I brought to him the kindness I had craved,
The empathy that been so elusive.
Pleasant. Though regret about the past plagued.
Not realizing that I had transformed into
the closure that I lost, when I learnt about the
tragedy of all of us. Oh! I lost it when
I learnt about the tragedy of all of us.
Glancing at the mirror, I saw someone better.
No more Stygian horns, no nightly silent sobs.
My soul became a hammer, and it split the world
asunder. And once more, I was a boy. Again.

title: Limerence
author: –M (م)
excerpt: Your eyes burn with silver light like the moon,
imageAlt: Cover image for Limerence
content: Your eyes burn with silver light like the moon,
Flaws so magical they become the reason hearts surrender.
Those brown hues are the home I want to return to every night.
Let them embrace me, while my soul melts against yours.
The ones who behold the entire galaxy,
are those mirrors of heavens I haven’t yet drowned into in real form.
But one day, this soul,
yearns to never look away from your eclipse pools.
You are the soul, the one I never want to give away.
The verse I never want to finish reading.
The dawn horizons I would burn my skin in.
The lanterns for the depths of my broken heart.
The places where I want to be yet cradled.
I saw your dark browns,
lost in every wave,
forgotten where I had started,
unreachable to where you have ended.
And now I understand why people crave light.
Because some eyes carry it —
the way the moon carries the sun.

title: How Would You Prove It?
author: Zahraa Zee
excerpt: I
imageAlt: Cover image for How Would You Prove It?
content: I
Brass. Green with age where the weather had got it, numbers raised up off the surface.
"The address…the address plate…”
The window going in, not shattering but folding into itself, like ice. Something spreading across a
carpet, taking its time.
“blood…theft…”
Then the man on his back with his mouth open and a knife standing straight up out of his chest
like something planted there on purpose.
“cold-blooded murder…sad…so sad…”
And underneath all of it, every time, somebody humming.
…please help, HELP!"
Emma woke up with a start. Her heart was frantic in her chest. After a bit, she cooled down and
approached the bedside table.
"Damned sleeping pills didn't work."
The hot weather made the shirt stick to her sweaty back. These windless, normal nights had
been showing her the same nightmare over and over again. Emma had approached several
psychiatrists, begging them to make a diagnosis. Every one of them had listened to her for
eleven minutes and then explained, kindly, that it was a hallucination. That she was nineteen.
That her age didn't support serious things.
She had stopped arguing about a year ago. There is no point arguing with someone who has
already decided what you are.
The same thing over and over again. A movie she'd grown tired of watching. A house, an
address, a murder. She looked at the bulletin board above her desk, a medicinal chart, and the
crossed numbers of each doctor who prescribed her anti-depressants. Eleven of them crossed
out one after another in different pens.
The twelfth was not crossed out. Three weeks old, written in her own hand, still waiting to
disappoint her.
It felt like someone was behind these nightmares, someone had been trying to show her their
story, an illusion, trying to drive her mad on purpose. And it was taking something out of her that
she could not put back. She had stopped recognising her own wrists.
"If they won't fix me, I'll fix myself. It's nothing new, I've done this before."
Emma snatched up her blankets as concealed anger consumed her and tried to go back to
sleep. Bits of the address flew in her mind.
II
Emma had walked these roads for nineteen years so she let her feet carry her. A dull ache
penetrated her forehead for the lack of sleep last night. She had been thinking about the dream
more than ever. She seemed to be forgetting some crucial parts, it kept rearranging itself most
frustratingly, as though somebody were moving the furniture around in there while she slept.
A sad story really, the accidental murder of a man by a thief who only wanted to steal the
antique through the broken window. No one inquired about the dead man. Yes, she had to find
him, bury his dead body, and give him the peace he deserved.
Emma checked her phone. Twenty days since she'd fainted at a party. Eighteen days since the
last text message from her friends. Seven days since–
"OWh! Oh gosh…"
She fell face-first onto the path, wincing as a burning sensation flowed from her knees. With
great difficulty, she stood up, supporting herself on a wooden fence. This was an unfamiliar
alleyway, she'd never seen these houses before. All of them foreboding, with empty windows.
And the house in front of her, undoubtedly the one from her dreams.
The wooden monster worn with age seemed to be in some sort of meditation. She could almost
hear its soft snores in sleep. Brown things blew into the air that at first seemed to be leaves but
were really pieces of the plaster. A big front yard separated the house from the wooden fence.
She told herself she was mistaken. Every old house looks like every other old house. She told
herself this quite firmly, and then she looked at the gatepost.
The plate was brass and green with age. The numbers were raised.
She did not want to open the gate. She was simply on the other side of it, and the gate was
swinging behind her with a scratching noise that made her skin crawl.
She hobbled to the front of the house and knocked politely. It seemed to her that it would be the
proper thing to do. She had a pounding headache and only thought of her dream.
"Hello? Is someone there?" she yelled, unsure of a reply. Grabbing the knob, she gave a hard
push. A putrid smell of decay filled her nostrils as the door gave way. She could see light ahead.
One door revealed a drawing room that was supposedly the scene of the crime. Just like in her
dream, the big window was broken and the so-called antique was on the floor. The blood stains
decorated the carpet like some pattern but…there was no dead body.
Emma felt uneasy. A humming voice was penetrating her ears, and she realised with a slow and
sickening clarity that she had heard it before, every night, for a year, and had never once
thought to wonder whose it was.
Scanning the corridor, she saw a room at the far end. She felt sure it was the bedroom.
As the door swung open, her heart hammered in her chest as if her guts already knew what was
inside. There was the dead man on the bed. He lay sprawled, his arms hanging over the
bedsides, his blood staining the white bedsheets. The knife protruded from his chest.
It disturbed her, it disturbed the whole natural scene of death, the knife like some unnatural
force that could rob a life. A delicious cool was settling inside her, but curiosity nagged at the
back of her mind. She felt horrifyingly mesmerised by the man's milky white eyes.
Emma surveyed the room. There was little or no furniture, save for the bed, a chair, some rope,
and a bookshelf. She stared at the large bookshelf on the wall, which through some abnormality
seemed to be pushed forward on one side. The humming voice started again in her mind.
Feeling strange, she tried to move it.
A dark room was revealed. She felt around for switches. Catching something ovoid in her hand,
she gave it a hard pull. The room lit up.
Directly in front of her was a rusted steel table. Beside it was a smaller table with surgical
instruments laid out in a row, largest to smallest, the way a person lays things out when they
intend to find them again in a hurry. The wall up front was lined with assortments of knives.
She had seen instruments arranged like that somewhere. In daylight. On a tray. The thought
arrived and left before she could stop it.
Her eyes fell to the left of the room, where the whole wall was a board.
Several pictures, pieces of paper, building plans, blueprints, and newspaper clippings were held
up by threaded tacks, each thread running out to a person's face.
She looked closer, which was the mistake.
The first one she recognised was the girl from the petrol station posters, the one whose mother
went on the news in a green cardigan. Emma had watched that broadcast. She had felt sorry for
about four minutes and then gone to dinner.
The second was a boy from two districts over. There had been a search party. There had been a
hashtag.
The third she did not recognise, and the fourth she did, and then she stopped counting, because
the wall went on, and they were all facing her, and each one was still smiling in the photograph
somebody's family had chosen.
Beside every picture, a small yellow sticky note. On every note, a smiley face, drawn carelessly,
the way you doodle while you are on the phone.
Every victim?
Her eyes travelled along the wall and stopped.
Except…her own.
MY OWN?
Her photograph was near the end, slightly lower than the others, the paper gone soft at the
corner from handling. She was wearing a blue top. She had worn the blue top to an
appointment. She had worn it to an appointment and nowhere else, because it had a stain on
the cuff and she had thrown it away afterwards, and she remembered throwing it away, and she
remembered which bin.
The photograph had been taken from the side, and slightly above, as though whoever took it
had been sitting across a desk from her.
There was a sticky note beside her picture too.
It was blank.
Something started to bother her very much. There were blood prints all over the floor. As if
something had been dragged. It looked like rust on the bigger table. Upon closer inspection, it
was dried blood and mucus.
Fear completely swallowed her, as did the distant humming voice. Fear immobilized her.
She turned around to go back but her eyes slowly fell to the right wall. A small rectangular
mirror, blurry with dust. She could see the fear in her face. But directly behind her was another
face. A crooked smile with black teeth and bulging white eyes.
She gave a bloodcurdling scream as the apparition behind her raised a knife, the very one that
was stuck in its chest, and a gaping hole replaced it. She swerved madly, making for the
entrance of the secret slaughter room. And at the same time, the dead man struck.
She could feel the knife as it barely skinned her arm. The dead body of the man was no longer
on the bed but she did not care and did not think. She forced herself out of the room, the
humming voice at its peak, hitting her head on a loose plank in the doorway. For only a second,
Emma could feel her life ebbing away.
Somehow, she made it to the door and pushed herself out. Trying to balance herself as much as
she could, she walked, barely making it to the front yard. She clutched her head, trying to numb
the pain.
Everything felt quiet now, with no humming voice, only the sunlight and the grass under her feet.
She looked back one last time. There, staring straight at her through the broken window, was
the dead man. His soiled nightclothes, the knife now in his chest again, the nightmarish smile,
the white eyes looking straight at her.
No longer being able to hold herself together, she fainted.
III
A beep woke Emma from her deep slumber. At first, she understood and felt nothing. Slowly,
everything came into focus. A white ceiling, something pushed into her nose, and a constant
beeping.
Quite annoyed, she tried to move her arms.
They refused to oblige and lay dormant beside her, and she groaned at how heavy her body felt.
She tried again. Her fingers answered, a little, far away, as though they belonged to somebody
in the next room. Her arms did not.
Looking around, she realized she was in a hospital room. She was laid down on a bed, no
longer in her clothes but basked in complete white, her blond hair enveloping her face. She
blinked a few times in confusion.
A nurse came inside. Ecstatic to see her awake, she left again to fetch a doctor.
Emma wanted to tell somebody about the house. She had the whole thing ready. The board, the
notes, the photograph in the blue top. She had been rehearsing it since before she opened her
eyes, and she knew how it would go, because she had said true things to doctors before.
Eleven times. In eleven different rooms.
The door opened.
He wore a blue shirt and a white coat and a stethoscope around his neck, and he was
humming.
Milky white eyes with black pupils piercing into hers. The same crooked smile she saw through
the broken window.
Three weeks ago he had written her a prescription, and she had copied his number onto the
board above her desk, in her own handwriting, and she had not crossed it out.
He closed the door behind him with his foot.
"Nobody believed you," he said. "I know.”

title: A Memory of a River or a River of Memory?
author: Syed Raiyan Nuri Reza
excerpt: I see a woman by the river. She is covered in some tar-like black sludge. Scars and wounds mark her skin. Some of the open cuts are raw and bleeding, oozing...is that ichor? Yet, s
imageAlt: Cover image for A Memory of a River or a River of Memory?
content: I see a woman by the river. She is covered in some tar-like black sludge. Scars and
wounds mark her skin. Some of the open cuts are raw and bleeding, oozing...is that ichor?
Yet, she sits serene and poised in her frayed and grimy sari. There is an unmistakable gravity
to her presence. And, I feel a pull towards her, an inexplicable sense of having seen her
before.
"Forgive me if this comes across as a strange question. But, do I know you?" I ask
timidly. The woman turns and looks at me with sorrowful eyes of deep, deep black-blue. I
swear the fathomless depths of those black-blue eyes hold the river and ocean and, therein, all
manners of ancient things dwell. She speaks but I cannot recognize her tongue.
"I am really sorry...l do not understand", I say.
She smiles a melancholic smile and gestures me to sit. So, I take a spot by her and, in
her aura, immediately feel a cleansing spring-water coolness. A pleasant relief from the
suffocating humid heat of summer. She gazes towards the horizon and I follow suit. The
width of the river conceals the far bank. Instead, the black-blue river melts into the vault of
the azure sky above. I can make out the launches and dingis sailing the calm waters, ferrying
souls to and from and around Chandpur. Here and there on the river, the green patches of
foliage, mostly Shoibal and there is also Kochuripana, and the occasional piece of flotsam.
The woman begins to speak in a tongue that I realize with a bone-deep certitude that I once
knew. I listen closely to her words as she goes on and on. Her words sound foreign. Yet, I
recognize the singsong of birds and melody of lapping waves and pitter-patter of monsoon
rains and in the depths of my murky memories something stirs. Her words catch like
fishhooks, tugging loose fragments of a buried past and reeling them to the surface. And, so I
remember a time when I could tell a Doyel from Myna just from their chirps and talk with
ilish and speak with banyan trees. Back when I knew my mother tongue and vernacular of
this land and its soils and rivers and flora and fauna. When I would sit right here and chat
with this woman. Nameless but no stranger.
And, soon, nameless no more. The memory of her name finally dislodges from the
depths and bubbles up to the surface of my mind. Or, at least, the memory of one of the many
names people called her across the ages. Perhaps, she is even older than when there was a
necessity for names. When the world was new to us and simply pointing sufficed.
Nevertheless, I remember, I remember now. Enough at least to name the woman beside me
with her singsong voice and petrichor scent. I turn towards her and, alas, behold her true
form. Have the scales fallen from my eyes? Or did my remembrance restore some vigor to
her? Her skin, resplendently brown; shining golden in the afternoon sun. Her hair, a wavy
lustrous black. That once tattered sari of hers, now of the finest muslin.
"Meghna?", I say. Before she even replies, I taste familiarity in the twisting and
turning of my tongue and its flicker on my palate that shapes my breath into the utterance of
her name. She breaks her gaze from the horizon and looks me in the eyes, this time there is
twinkle instead of melancholy.
'Obosheshe amake chinte perechho
"Of course, I know you... ", I reply. I hesitate, searching for the right word, but the
word I seek eludes me like a slippery eel. So all I say is, "old friend". Someday, soon, I will
remember that the once-forgotten word that I sought was dosto.

title: The Realm of Nothingness
author: Tas.R
excerpt: When he opened his eyes, he was sprawled on his back in a white room, a bare white ceiling staring back at him. He had no idea why he was here or how he had gotten here.

content: When he opened his eyes, he was
sprawled on his back in a white room, a
bare white ceiling staring back at him.
He had no idea why he was here or how
he had gotten here.
He had never even been here before.
At least, that was what he could
remember. He had a strange feeling that
this place was not entirely unknown to
him, but he had no memories to show
for it. For a person in an odd room he
had never visited before, he felt
strangely calm. As if time had stopped
and there was nothing and no one
except him, existing in this very moment.
He sat up. The room was a dull white
from ceiling to floor, completely devoid
of any furnishings, entrances or exits.
The color was not the pristine white of
an angel's wing or the elegant white of a
pearl — rather, the color reminded him of
a dying person. Not necessarily when
the heart ceases to circulate blood, but
when it ceases to beat for the people
one loved. The mind rotting away long
before the body.
He was calm on the surface, but deep
inside, a dread slowly seeped into a
small part of his mind and spread like
blood spreading through water. He was
scared—scared because he knew that
he was the person that was dying.
Pushing down his fear, he looked
around. There was a window across
from him. He stood up, slowly walked
towards the window, and dropped
himself down on the floor right in front
of it. He watched the slightly translucent
white curtains sway as a gentle breeze
blew in from the outside. When the
curtains went still, the thin fabric
revealed the outline of bars of the
window.
As far as he could see, there was
nothing but more white nothingness
outside the window. He knew that he
should have been terrified, frantically
searching for a way out of this place, but
he didn't want to do any of that. As if
something from deep within himself, a
child, told him to stay here.
So he stayed there. Sitting with his
knees drawn to his chest, eyes glued to
the window. The white nothingness
seemed to resemble his own future—
vague and unpredictable. Maybe if he
looked hard enough, he would find
something in the distance.
Or maybe there wasn't a future for him.
Maybe it wasn't all too bad; he enjoyed
the tranquil atmosphere in the room
although it felt terribly empty. He felt so
alone; a lone cliff overlooking a calm
sea.
The silence of the room was broken by
the soft rustle of paper-thin wings.
A small butterfly flew in through the
window. Eyes tracking the creature, he
held his finger out and the butterfly
obediently perched on it, fluttering its
plain, faded yellow wings. It was the
only thing that had any color in the room.
He didn't know why the butterfly was
here or how it had found him, but he was
glad that it did. Now he didn't feel so
alone anymore.
Perhaps this was how people felt before
passing away. There was no pain, he felt
no remorse, only a misplaced sense of
calm. Almost detached.
"Thank you," he told the butterfly.
The butterfly only fluttered its delicate
wings in response. He was grateful for
its presence. At least he could now pass
with a witness, no matter how small it
was. Sure, none of his friends or family
were here, but at least the butterfly was.
"It's time for me to go," he said to no one
in particular.
"No, not yet," whispered the butterfly.
